Mr. Speaker, when this was introduced it was not my intention to say anything at this stage as I was well aware that there are several hon. members of our small group here who are far better qualified than I to speak on matters pertaining to agriculture. However, the opposition to the bill has covered such wide ground and has been so inconsistent at times that I felt I should add my mite, if for no other reason than to answer some of the charges which have been levelled against us in this corner of the house. I think almost every hon. member who has spoken on the bill has stated that it is of very great importance. According to those on my right, it is important for its ill effects, while on the government side of the house it is maintained of course that it is important for its beneficial effects. As a matter of fact I believe that one member, my hon. friend from Nelson (Mr. Stitt), went so far as to say that it was revolutionary and, moreover, that he was glad to take part in this particular revolution. I appreciate that for my hon. friend from Nelson to speak about revolution is much safer than it is for me. I would suggest to him however that he be careful because if the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) hears of it he will certainly use it against him.

I am not sure whether the bill is as important as either its opponents or its friends say it is, but I am quite satisfied that it is significant. It is significant in that it shows that an appreciation of the social and economic developments of the past few years are at last percolating through the mental equipment of some people. It is significant also because it is evidently becoming-

The bill to me is significant because it is evidently becoming apparent to the advocates of rugged individualism that that very desirable virtue is rapidly leading to ragged individualism.
I favour this bill in principle. I am not saying of course that it is perfect nor that I will vote for it if it is not improved, but I will certainly vote for its second reading because I do agree with the principle. I am in favour of the principle of cooperation. For almost a quarter of a century I have belonged to the trade union movement and I understand and realize the benefits that have accrued to the working class through their association in trade unions. Unfortunately compulsion had sometimes to be used and perhaps unfortunately also there are compulsory clauses in this bill. But I believe that the farmer himself is beginning to realize -the benefits of cooperation and has come to the conclusion that a certain measure of compulsion may be necessary to impress upon the more shortsighted in his own class that it is essential for them to cooperate for the welfare of all.
In my opinion the bill has become necessary for the same reason -that it has become necessary to regulate traffic on city streets and even on country roads. We restrict the freedom of the individual on our streets and roads because it is necessary in the interests and for the safety of all who use the streets and roads that such restriction should be enforced.
I think it was the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) who pointed out when introducing the bill that the position of the farmer had changed very considerably during the last generation or so. He pointed out I believe that it was not so long ago when the farmer was producing on his own farm most of the stuff consumed by himself and his family. It was consumed on the farm. What he sold or exchanged he sold to or exchanged direct with the consumer. Now I think we

Marketing Act-Mr. Maclnnis
must realize that the farmer's position has indeed changed considerably, particularly within the last twenty-five years. To-day he is not turning out a complete product; that is to say, he is taking some part in the production of a socially produced commodity. He is producing not for his own consumption and for the consumption of his family but for a market, and the article or commodity he is producing is not finally finished until it has reached the ultimate consumer somewhere within the four comers of the earth.
In recent years the farmer has passed through a stage comparable I think to that which the handicraft worker of other days passed through at the time of the industrial revolution. As a matter of fact he is passing through an agricultural revolution. I think it was Sir Arthur Salter who, in his book Recovery, pointed out that if there had been no financial crisis at all nor an industrial crisis there would have been an agricultural crisis. He also pointed out that the methods which the farmer followed to overcome his difficulties were different from those pursued by financial and industrial interests. He said that when the price of farm commodities fell, the farmer, in order to make up for the loss of revenue through falling prices, instead of reducing the quantity of his product going on the market increased it, with the result that there was a further fall in prices, and so on.
In my opinion the position of the farmer to-day is very close to that of his brother worker in the city. May I for a few moments try to show the similarity. Living under a system of capitalism in which, in order to live, everyone must have something to sell and not only have something to sell but also to find a buyer, the farmers and the industrial workers find themselves in very much the same position. Let us take the industrial worker first. By and large the city and town workers have nothing to sell but their ability to labour, and when they find someone to buy their labour they are said to have found a job. But note this. They have no claim to ownership in what they will produce with their labour. They sell their labour power at its market price, depending like all other commodities to some extent on the law of supply and demand; but what they produce belongs not to themselves but to the person or corporation buying their labour and paying the price therefor-wages. What they produce is left in the plant or factory when they have done their day's work.
The exploitation of the industrial worker is easy to see. I remember years ago when we used to discuss how the industrial worker and
the farmer were exploited. It was easy to see that the industrial worker was exploited at the point of production, but it was not so easy to find where the farmer was exploited. He did not sell his labour direct to anyone. He was a man of property who owned land and machinery and stock of various kinds. But I think it has become more clear since that time how he is being exploited. One thing of course is clear, that he does not sell his labour direct to an employer, but turns that labour, by the use of his land, his machinery and his stock, into various commodities depending upon the particular form of agricultural production in which he is engaged. If he is a grain farmer he turns it into various kinds of grain; if he is a dairy farmer he turns it into dairy products, and if he is a fruit farmer, he turns it into various kinds of fruits. But note this: that the moment he has done that he is under the same compulsion to do what the industrial worker had to do, that is to find someone to buy his commodities. That is where his difficulties begin. He has no say in setting the price of what he has to sell and no say in setting the price of what he has to buy. He is selling in a market that, so far as he is concerned, is absolutely uncontrolled, and on the other hand he is buying in a market that is absolutely controlled. He is, as a matter of fact, selling in a market that is not only not controlled but is sometimes rigged and manipulated against him, and he is buying in a market that is not only controlled by the producers of manufactured articles but is also protected by tariffs of various kinds. So it will be readily seen that the farmer is exploited through the market.
We hear a great deal these days about confiscation and the dangers of confiscation. Let me say that the farmer is confiscated annually at the end of every year because everything except a bare living is taken away from him through the market.
I am quite satisfied that the bill in its present state is not perfect, but I suppose nothing is perfect when it is first conceived. We know that the automobile of to-day is very different from the first automobile and that the airship of to-day is very different from the first airship that was tried out by the Wright brothers. After my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) had spoken on this bill a week or so ago, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) followed and castigated us in this corner for supporting this bill. According to him we< were falling into the Conservative net; I believe the simile he used was that of the spider and the fly. Well, I

Quite so. But that does not mean, Mr. Speaker, that we are not going to support any good measure that comes before this house regardless of whether it is introduced by Liberals or Conservatives. So far as I am personally concerned, I made one promise and one only to the electors in my constituency, and that was that I would support any measure which I thought would be to the advantage of those I represent, and on the other hand, that I would oppose any measure which I thought would be to their disadvantage regardless of who introduced it.
The leader of the opposition pretends to be greatly concerned over the undermining of our parliamentary institutions. I think anyone who keeps his ear to the ground these days and realizes how parliaments and democratic institutions have disappeared in other countries must also have realized that they have disappeared because they failed to function to improve the conditions of the people of those countries, and if we in this house of parliament are going to waste our time in mere talk, I think the people will get tired of parliament and use some other means of making available to themselves the great wealth of this country.
May I say to the leader of the opposition that nothing could be more detrimental to the dignity and usefulness of parliament than his own opposition to every measure good, bad or indifferent that is brought before parliament. In his opposition to this bill he went back to the thirteenth century to the time of Magna Charta, and in extolling the rights and privileges conferred on the people by that great document he pointed out that they were endangered by this bill. Now, to be historically accurate, the Magna Charta did not confer any rights or privileges upon the great mass of the British people; it conferred rights and privileges upon only a certain class, upon the barons, the ruling class of that time. So far as the great mass of the people is concerned, they never had any economic rights at 
that time and consequently any political or legal rights for them were quite useless. The leader of the opposition is so enmeshed and so obsessed with the letter of the law that he has lost sight of the spirit of the law; he is so .taken up with the question of legal justice that he is overlooking a greater and more fundamental thing, that is, social justice. He fails to realize that until we have social and economic justice, legal and political justice will be of very little benefit to us. Let me give a little information to the house in regard to the condition of the working class in Great Britain upon whom, according to the leader of the opposition, the Magna Charta conferred such great privileges and benefits. I am speaking not only of the time when Magna Charta was signed, but of conditions six hundred or more years later, or about one hundred years ago. The leader of the opposition quoted from Green's History of England; I shall quote from another book which I believe is a classic of its kind, H. de B. Gibbons' Industrial History of England. Speaking of the condition of the working class in 1834 he says:
But then came the great continental wars and the industrial revolution; and it is a sad but significant fact that, although the total wealth of the nation vastly increased at the end of last century and the beginning of this, none of that wealth came into the hands of the labourers, but went entirely into the hands of the great landlords and new capitalist manufacturers, or was spent in the enormous expenses of foreign war.
Then he says:
Moreover, labour was now more than ever dependent on capital, and the individual labourer was thoroughly under the heel of his employer.
Thoroughly under the heel of his employer despite the privileges of Magna Charta.
This, it will be remembered, was the result of the system of assessment of wages under which the justices of the peace, including of course chiefly manufacturers and landowners, fixed the wages of labour for their own districts, and fixed them at so low a figure that they had nearly always to be supplemented out of the rates paid by the general public. The labourer had no redress, for all combination in the form now known as trades unions was suppressed, and his condition sank to the lowest depth of poverty and degradation.
You notice that at that time the labourers' wages and keep had to be supplemented out of the relief funds of that day, if I may use that term. The same things is happening in the Dominion of Canada at the present time, where the labourers must be sustained to some exteDt out of the relief funds of the

Marketing Act-Mr. Maclnnis
municipalities, as came out before the price spread and mass buying committee a little while ago.
Now we go a little further:
What made the condition of the labourers worse still, was the fact that they could neither go from one place to another to seek work, nor could they combine in industrial partnerships for their mutual interests.
What wonderful privileges these people had, when they could not go from one place to another; if they did not like the master they had they could not go and look for another. Now they blame the workers for not going because forsooth they have more of them than they need. Adam Smith said:
We have no acts of parliament against combining to lower the price of work, but many against combining to raise it.
At another place he said:
The workmen, had, of course, no political influence; they could only show their discontent by riots and rick burnings.
So much for the privileges conferred upon the British people by Magna Charta.
Then the right hon. gentleman went further and pointed out that nearly all of the improvements that have come to the working class have come through the Liberal party. That does not agree at all with H. de B. Gibbons. At page 184 of his book he says:
These unions of workmen cried out for the restriction of non-adult labour to ten hours a day, and the Conservative party, who were chiefly interested in the land and not in the mills, supported them readily against the manufacturers, who were mainly Liberals and Radicals.
Then at page 185 he goes on to say:
It is curious to notice how these acts were passed. They all showed the steady advance of the principle of state interference with labour; a doctrine most distasteful to the old Ricardian school of economists, even when that interference was made in the interests of the physical and moral well-being, not only of the industrial classes, but of the community at large. Hence the economists of the day aided the manufacturers in opposing these acts to the utmost of their power, and the laws passed were due to the action of the Tories and landowners. Lord Shaftesbury, Fielden. Oastler, and Sadler were all Tories, though they were accused of being socialists. They were supported by the landed gentry.
We hear just the same thing to-day. Everyone who even suggests that there should be an improvement in the condition of the working masses is termed a socialist or a bolshevist or a communist right away. It does not make any difference whether he belongs to the group here or on the government side of the house.
Then we go a little further. I wish the hon. member for Weyburn were in his seat.
John Bright especially distinguished himself by his violent denunciation of the Ten Hours bill, which he characterized' as "one of the worst measures ever passed in the shape of an act of the legislature."
That was before this bill was introduced, of course. John Bright was the great apostle of free trade, yet he was strongly opposed to any improvement in the condition of the working class through reduction of hours, or possibly increase of wages.

Quite so, that is why I wish he were here.
Let me give you one other instance of the privileges conferred upon the working class by Magna Charta. In 1834 there were tried, convicted and transported from England to Australia six agricultural labourers. Among them were George Loveless and James Loveless, brothers. I understand that the descendants of these two brothers are living at present somewhere in Ontario. The crime of these men was that they tried to organize the agricultural workers. George Loveless in court made this statement:
We have injured no man's reputation, character, person or property, we were uniting to preserve ourselves, our wives and children from utter degradation and starvation.
It is a long way from prosecuting people for organizing, to passing laws to compel them to organize for their own good. We certainly are moving, and I hope in the right direction. The judge in passing sentence on them said:
Not for anything you have done, or, as I can prove, that you intended to do, but for example to others, I consider it my duty to pass the sentence of seven years penal transportation across His Majesty's high seas to each and every one of you.
So much then for Magna Charta and the favours it bestowed upon the British people.

One of the terms of the charter was that:
To no man will we sell or deny or delay right or justice.
I wonder who it was that denied or delayed right and justice to these people even up to seven hundred or more years after Magna Charta was signed? The very class which at the point of the sword compelled King John to sign the charter.

Marketing Act-Mr. Maclnnis
In 1842, coming still further down, I find this in a report made by the children's employment committee, describing the employment of the children in the mines:
Chained, belted, harnessed like dogs in a go-cart, black, saturated with wet and more than half-naked, crawling upon their hand's and feet and dragging their heavy loads behind them, they present an appearance indescribably disgusting and unnatural.
That was in 1842. I wonder who delayed right and justice to these children, and who is denying them right and justice to-day? The very successors of the barons who wrested the charter from King John at the point of the sword.
So much for the leader of the opposition. Now let me turn to something more pleasant. But before turning to that I notice that Sir Basil Blackett in a certain speech made a little time ago on the necessity of cooperation in industry, made this statement:
I know there are a great many people who quarrel with this doctrine, who hanker after the good old times. They will not believe that Queen Victoria is dead. What they say is, "if only the state would stop interfering, if it would stop doles to the unemployed, if it would stop interference with trade and commerce, if it would adopt complete free trade, then all would be well."
Then he goes on to say:
But would it?
I wish someone would take it upon himself to tell the leader of the opposition that Queen Victoria is dead.
Now let me come to something more pleasant. We are told that no matter what progress the C.C.F. may make elsewhere it will never make progress in the province of Quebec. Mr. Speaker, I trust the hon. member who has just taken his seat will not think it discourteous on my part if I do not attempt to follow him in the arguments he has brought forward in connection with the bill, because in the time at my disposal I intend to approach the matter from an angle entirely different from that pursued by the hon. member.
Having the honour to represent in this house a constituency in which the majority of the people are engaged in agricultural pursuits, my action in supporting the second reading of this measure, namely one to improve the methods and practices of marketing of natural products in Canada and in export trade, will, I am confident, meet with the approval of a majority of these people. The people in my constituency, irrespective of political leanings-whether they be Conservative, Liberal or supporters of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation-[DOT] desire that this legislation may become law, and that such condition may be brought about as quickly as possible. They realize that from the application of the provisions contained in this measure great good may accrue to the western farmers. I desire therefore to approach my discussion of the matter from the point of view of the farmer of southern Alberta. Even at the risk of repeating some of the arguments already made I desire to place on record the attitude of the men living in that section of Canada which I have the honour to represent. I should like to devote the latter half of the time allotted to me to an exploration of the possibilities of our receiving some assistance from the bill, and particularly the extent to which two important branches of agriculture carried on in southern Alberta may be affected.
First may I inquire as to why it is necessary for us to have this legislation, and why is it termed legislation which is urgently needed?
My first answer would be that the farmers of Canada, together with farmers throughout the whole world, have suffered severely from the drop in commodity prices. I have before me a comparison showing the figure for today as compared with that of the year 1926, and it indicates that farm products in Canada have declined by 47-7 per cent. There is much less decline to-day than there was one year or even two years ago. I find that wheat has fallen to-day to the: extent of 55-7 per cent, giving an index figure of 44'3. When we are dealing with wheat we are dealing with the most important product of western Canada. When we turn to manufactured goods we have to-day the figure of 76 per cent as compared with 100 in 1926. The purchasing power of the dollar has increased 36-7 per cent.
Although the farmers in Canada and the world over have received for their products prices which were unremunerative, yet having to meet the demands of their creditors they have increased rather than reduced their production. They have tried to make up in volume what they lost in value. As a result the world market has been flooded; it has been overloaded with goods and commodity prices have fallen to a very low level. Our domestic market suffered similarly, and many examples could be given to show the wastage which resulted from lack of a definite marketing plan or system of marketing.
My second reason for believing that the present legislation is necessary is that the countries of the world have placed restrictions against the exchange of goods between nations. What are the policies which, having been placed in operation, have restricted international trade? Before the war the most important method by which we restricted imports was through the instrumentality of tariff duties. Since the war, however, various other methods have been adopted and used extensively. The type of restrictions applicable to trade in agricultural products can be divided into two major classes, the first of which consists of import restrictions. Under that heading I make four subdivisions, namely milling regulations, import quotas, licensing of importers and foreign exchange. The second major class is that of export aids and restrictions, and again I make four subdivisions, namely, commercial treaties, export bounties, improvement by inspection in the quality or standard of the article, and restriction of exports.
The effect of these restrictions has been felt in every part of the world, and in that statement Canada must be included. The bureau
2708	COMMONS
Marketing Act-Mr. Stewart (Lethbridge)
of statistics of the League of Nations records a loss of twenty-five per cent in volume of world trade, certainly old trade lanes have disappeared and very few new ones have taken their place. These restrictions have had such an effect upon world trade that various countries of the world have found it necessary to pass legislation to effect control of production, marketing and prices. I have before me a file giving the number and names of measures passed by various countries, and enumerating the legislative acts passed to effect control of production, marketing and prices. These figures indicate that thirty-six of the leading countries of the world have passed about one hundred and fifty pieces of legislation similar to that now before this house. I shall not weary the house by giving the names of the countries, but should like to place upon the record what has been done in two of the leading nations of the World. First, in connection with France, we have milling regulations in November, 1929, import quotas in September, 1931, import licences in November, 1931, flax and hemp subsidies in July, 1931, and March, 1932, government purchases of tobacco in December, 1931, seasonal tariffs in March, 1932, and a stabilization decree in October, 1932. It is quite evident from that list that France is not anxious that any imports of any kind shall enter that country.
In connection with Great Britain we have the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1931, the Wheat Act of 1932, the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1933, and the Agricultural Marketing Act of Northern Ireland of 1933.
What means are provided within this measure to assist in overcoming the difficulties about which I have spoken? First, what does the measure offer towards a solution of the financial troubles with which our farmers are faced? May I say that none has a more intimate knowledge of those troubles than has the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and the members of his cabinet. I think the executive were convinced long ago that the suggestions put forward by speakers at the Ottawa conferences that the only way in which to restore prosperity to the world was to increase wholesale commodity prices were sound statements. After a careful survey the government were convinced that the best way to assist the farmer was to give him an opportunity to market his goods in an orderly manner. During the last few days we have been told on several occasions that the farmer sells most of his products in the domestic market. It is therefore necessary that some regulation or

provision should be incorporated into this bill in order to assist the farmer in the marketing of his goods in Canada. I find that such a system is provided by this bill. First, there is the provision whereby we may prevent the manipulation of prices so that in the future there will not be a drop of two cents in the price of hogs within a week, as has happened recently, and that without any apparent reason. Second, the government will have the power to regulate the spread in prices, as a result of which I feel the farmer will receive a larger portion of the consumer's dollar. Third, we will have the power to take surpluses off the market; if there happens to be an excess of a product at any one time, the government will be able to appoint an ageijt to take such surplus off the market, store it and return it to the market when an opportunity is found. .
With regard to the passing of these 150 acts by thirty-six countries, I should like to ask the house if under these circumstances we should remain idle and if, through a fear of violating the Magna Charta of 1215, we should allow these conditions from without to destroy us without making any effort for our preservation. I feel that the government have the support of the majority of the people of Canada and one of the reasons why they have this support is the fact that this is a government of action. The government is alive to world conditions which affect the welfare of our people and is also alive to our domestic difficulties. The government has not failed us in this difficult situation but has produced a bill which will help us to solve the marketing problems of this time.
The bill has two main principles as its foundation. First, there is the orderly marketing of our products, and, second, it enables us to protect ourselves against destructive action by other countries. I think the government should be congratulated for bringing forward this measure. Praise is particularly due to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) who has taken a very prominent part in the construction of the bill. He is an able Minister of Agriculture and has placed in operation many policies which have greatly assisted those engaged in the farming industry. I venture to predict that when his record is written his name in the history of Canada will be more intimately and closely associated with this bill than with any other of his agricultural activities. It is one of the greatest forward steps that has been taken in Canada for the past twenty years.
Many messages have been received by various hon. members from their constituents containing praise for the provisions of this

Marketing Act

Mr. Stewart (Lethbridge)
bill. We have received messages from cooperative organizations, from united farmer organizations, from boards of trade and other public bodies. I should like to place on Hansard some observations which I have gleaned from reading the London Times of April 3. It states:
The natural products marketing bill which the Canadian government has introduced into the federal parliament seems likely to become the principal issue in dominion politics.
So far as the Conservative party is concerned, we should be very glad to have that happen. The article continues:
It is a comprehensive measure applying to all primary products, except those of the mines, the principles which recent marketing legislation in Great Britain has applied to certain selected branches of agriculture.
We are applying the principles of the British act to the products of Canadian agriculture. The article continues:
It may be assumed that the American experiments in economic planning have not been without influence in Canada; but the bill is avowedly based on the British model. If it becomes law and is put into effective operation, Canadian farmers will be organized on the same lines as the British, and the discussion of common problems and the arrangement of satisfactory conditions for mutual aid will be proportionately easier.
That article contains two very important statements. First, it states that our bill is based on the British model. I have heard hon. gentlemen opposite say that they would vote for this measure if it were based on the British model. Here is a statement by the greatest paper published in the English language to the effect that it is based upon the British model. Second, it says that when this measure becomes law the farmers of Canada will 'be organized on the same basis and in the same manner as are the farmers under the British act and that they will be able to get together to discuss common problems and make arrangements for satisfactory conditions for mutual aid to one another. Is not this something in which this government should take great pride? The article closes with the following statement:
The endeavour will no doubt be accompanied with mistakes and maladjustments, with temporary losses and inconveniences, but, given perseverence and discipline, there can in the end be no surer way to stable prosperity.
I do not think it would be possible to find a more eloquent tribute to the provisions of this bill than that statement by the editor of the greatest British paper.
Under this bill a marketing board will supervise our exports and will endeavour to see that our products are standard in quality
and that there is a continuity and uniformity of supply. This will assist greatly in making a success of the Ottawa agreements.. Those agreements gave us what are now the only stable markets we possess. No matter what may be the results hoped for from this legislation, it is important that we should have it now when- we have only restricted markets. It is important that we should have it even though we should have unrestricted markets, but the legislation becomes more important when- we have but the one market. The more restricted our markets are, the more imperative it becomes that we retain them by orderly marketing methods and leave nothing to chance or fortune.
It has been stated by our political opponents that Canada suffers from the restricted market which has been brought about by the fiscal policies of this government, but the history and the dates upon which these restrictions were brought into force proves that these charges are without foundation. Let us consider the history of the trade relations between Canada and the United States. From 1913 to 1921 the Underwood tariff was in force in chat great country and we find that our domestic exports increased from S139,000,000 in 1913 to $542,000,000 in 1921. In 1921 we sent $192,000,000 worth of farm products to the United States, and of all our domestic exports to the United States 88-4 per cent entered that country free, so that we were operating under what would be practically a free trade policy.
The emergency tariff was applied in 1921 and then we had the Fordney-MoCumber tariff from 1922 to 1930. In other words, these policies were in operation when the Liberal government was in power in Canada, and what effect did they have on our exports? Instead of sending $190,000,000 a year of our farm products to the United States, as we had been doing from 1913 to 1921, our exports of farm products to that country dropped to $92,000,000 a year and less. So that while the Mackenzie King government held the reins of power we lost a valuable market for our agricultural products amounting to $100,000,000 a year.
Was it the fiscal policy of hon. gentlemen opposite that brought about this loss? If it is argued that we have lost markets, through our fiscal policy, surely the same argument holds good with respect to their loss of markets. Now the loss of that valuable agricultural market, combined with the restricted

wheat market which prevailed when we came in, had serious effects. The restricted wheat market bore fruit in 1930 by seed which was sown in 1925, when the restrictions were put into operation by European countries, and that is the situation which this government found with regard to our foreign markets when the Bennett administration came into power in August, 1930. So far as our foreign markets are concerned, one might say they at that time absolutely spelled ruin for us. But we had a prime minister who was a man of action and he took action in September, 1930. It was an honest effort to save our country, and it certainly has preserved the identity of Canada.
But what action did the former government take to prevent the loss of our agricultural products market in the United States? Did they retaliate or negotiate? Well, if they negotiated they certainly did not make much of a success of it judging by their record as given to this house in the speech delivered by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Lueh-kovich) several evenings ago. They did not negotiate because they lacked the weapon with which to do so; and, what was still worse, they publicly declared that they would not take that weapon into their own hands to compel negotiation. Instead, they said to the United States, "You may do what you like about restricting our exports of agricultural products into your markets, we will not retaliate." Above all, we were counselled not to do anything provocative towards the United States.
I find now that I must turn to local matters in so far as this bill may affect agriculture in the riding which I have the honour to represent. Section 12 has this marginal note, that the governor in council shall have:
Power to restrict importation of natural products which compete with regulated products.
Under the provisions of section 12 I believe that an important branch of agriculture, carried on in the irrigated areas, may receive much needed assistance. I refer to the desire of farmers living in these irrigation districts to have an increase in the acreage sown to sugar beets. Hon. members are well aware that we have 135,000,000 invested in irrigation projects by which we are able to supply irrigation for over 1,000,000 acres in southern Alberta. For many years we have demonstrated that we can grow sugar beets successfully. The cash returns from the sugar beet greatly exceed the returns which the farmer receives for his hay and grain crops. It is

necessary to reduce our wheat acreage, and our farmers are very anxious to replace wheat acreage with sugar beets, and instead of 14,000 acres of sugar beets to have 28,000 or 30,000. We have a market at our door. We supply but twenty-eight per cent of the sugar consumption of Saskatchewan and Alberta, the other sixty-two per cent coming from a refinery not located in either of those provinces but hundreds of miles away in the city of Vancouver, and our desire is to replace raw cane sugar, which is imported into this country from Fiji, with sugar from beets grown by Canadian farmers on Canadian soil.
This sugar beet product is equal to the cane product and sells at ten cents per' hundred pounds less than is commanded by cane sugar. I would submit the following facts to the house for consideration, so that hon. members may have a knowledge of the value of a factory to a community. In 1932, 2| per cent of the lands in the Lethbridge northern irrigation district contributed 24J per cent of the total value of farm products in that area of 100,000 acres, and 2\ per cent of the lands in the Lethbridge northern irrigation district in 1932 contributed 40 per cent of the cash value of the crops grown in that area. In the second place, in 1933, $1,634,000 was spent by the refinery at Raymond for beets, labour, freight and supplies, and it is claimed that the refinery greatly assists in maintaining a population of 10,000 souls. Thirdly, it has been my privilege to examine the contracts made by a privately owned corporation in the sale of lands to farmers. I have examined thirty-eight of these contracts, and after choosing four of the agreements at random I am able to give this information to the house. The four taken are for purchases of land in which the contract price of each amounts to between $4,000 and $4,500. I will take two farmers who have a contract for growing sugar beets and two who have not such contracts but are near neighbours. The first man with a sugar beet contract has, for a period of five years, averaged a payment of over $306 a year on the principal he owes the corporation. The second man with a contract, in the same period of years, has averaged a payment of over $360 a year. Let us turn to the other side of the picture. The first man who has no sugar beet contract has averaged a payment of $50.05 per annum and the second man has averaged a payment of $34.06 over a shorter term of years.
Now you can readily see which class of farmer will be able to discharge the contract he has entered into for the purchase of land from that irrigation company. You can

Marketing Act-Mr. Stewart (Lethbridge)
readily see which class of farmer it is who will soon be able to call his home and his farm his own. Is it any wonder that the farmer who has no beet contract, but who may be just as good a farmer as the man who has a beet contract, is most anxious that we should have an increase in our sugar beet acreage? I find in the Ottawa Citizen of April 27, a dispatch from London as follows:
London, April 26.-Sugar beet yield of nine tons to the acre has been obtained by British beet growers this year. Earl de la Warre, parliamentary secretary to the minister of agriculture, speaking at a meeting of the Sugar Beet Society in London to-night described this result as "amazing."
Britain could claim a yield equal in efficiency to any country except perhaps Holland, he added'.
The meeting also was told British sugar-producers were delivering sugar at a lower price than in any other country in the world, and one-quarter of the sugar consumed here was being produced in the United Kingdom.
That is a very fine record, but we have surpassed that by a large margin, for in 1932 on a 14.000 acreage sown to sugar beets we had an average yield of 10-7 tons peir acre. Furthermore, we had a sugar content of 18-41 per cent, the highest on the North American continent. Even last year, which was not a good one for sugar beet production, we had an average per ton yield of 9-3 per acre.
A delegation of men from all parts of Canada, from Ontario, Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan and other provinces who are interested in the extension of the sugar beet industry, met a committee of the cabinet on February 23, 1934, and stressed the great value of and the urgent need for more factories. They also dwelt upon the final paragraph of the report submitted by the select standing committee on agriculture which investigated the sugar beet industry, and reported to the house in 1932. I quote that paragraph:
Your committee further recommends, that if no successful attempt be made in the immediate future by the refineries to increase the facilities for the manufacturing of beet sugar, the government should take into consideration steps to accomplish that end.
That report was adopted unanimously by this house over two years ago, and since that time there has been no effort made by the refineries to increase or improve the facilities for the manufacture of beet sugar. I would therefore respectfully submit to the government that it is now high time it stepped in and took action.
Section 12 of the bill now before the house gives the governor in council power to impose quotas on imports of regulated products. So
far as regulated products are concerned, I may say that the sugar beet is a regulated product. Giving evidence before the committee in 1932, one of the farmers from Ontario was asked if he would like to grow more sugar beets. "Oh my, yes" he said, "just give us the opportunity." We are not allowed to grow any more sugar beets because the sugar refineries cannot take care of the production, and we are asking for an extension of their facilities in order that they may be able to take care of greater production.
I would say that no import lends itself more readily to the quota restrictions than raw cane sugar, for two reasons. First of all, because that import can be replaced by a Canadian product furnished by Canadian farmers, and in the long run it will not cost the consumer one cent more for the refined product which is equally as good as that which is derived from t)he raw cane. Secondly, there are but five industrial corporations interested in refining cane sugar. Might I add that the management of these corporations appear to have divided Canada into zones for distribution purposes and in these zones there is only one class or grade of sugar sold; there is no competition between companies. When application is made on behalf of these farmers, or when they make application themselves to the government, from t'he various parts of Canada that raw cane sugar be placed on a quota basis, I trust that their application will be received with the sympathy it rightly deserves and that the government will see to it that Humanity, spelled with a capital H; and I say that in all seriousness-receives the fair and kindly consideration it rightfully deserves. If a quota is applied, and we would urge that it should be applied, then I am certain that the sugar beet industry will receive the aid it now requires and that within two years we shall be supplying twenty-five per cent of the requirements of the Canadian people instead of the fourteen per cent which we now provide, and that instead of three sugar beet refineries in Canada we shall have five. I am as confident as I am sure that I am standing here, that in the not distant future fifty per cent of our sugar consumption in Canada will be supplied from the products of Canadian farms grown by Canadian farmers, and when that day comes it will be a day of rich blessing for the farmers of our land and the labourers of our country.
May I close by recalling to the attention of the house and the country the statement made by the London Times, a portion of which I have already read. I should like to conclude
Small Loan Company

with this warning, but also with this assurance as to the future of this act: "this endeavour will no doubt be accompanied by mistakes and maladjustments, with temporary losses and inconveniences, but, given perseverance and discipline, there can in the end be no surer way to stable prosperity."
At six o'clock the house took recess.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Weir (Melfort) for the second reading of Bill No. 51, to improve the methods and practices of marketing of natural products in Canada and in export trade, and to make further provisions in connection therewith.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
In rising to speak to this bill let me say at the outset that I differ from many members on this side of the house. But with many hon. members I realize and agree that the days of haphazard marketing of farm products have almost passed. We have come to the age of orderly marketing, which I believe to be necessary to-day in regard to most if not all our farm products. When I think of trying to maintain export markets for our farm products I realize the necessity of some such plan of orderly marketing. We have legislation to take care of quality and grades of many lines of agricultural produce, but I believe we shall have to go a step further and have uniformity of quality from one end of Canada to the other. Not only that, but having once obtained a market abroad that market will have to be retained by continuity of supply. I for one realize that the farmer has seen every other industry organized but his own. The farmer has for many years been forced to buy in the dearest market and to sell his goods in the cheapest market because of not having yet been able to combine or organize for the welfare of himself and his fellow farmers. In these days control is necessary. Farmers should not always leave it to others to market their goods, but every effort on the part of farmers to combine for the betterment of themselves and their class has been bitterly opposed by combines and interests concerned.
The present bill seems to me more of a regulating bill than a marketing bill. I am not altogether surprised at that, because we have recently learned that in Australia and New Zealand similar bills are being put into effect, due to the condition of affairs that has arisen in the old country in connection with agri-

Marketing Act-Mr. Reid
culture. As the premier of Australia is reported to have stated, it is far better to have regulation of agricultural exports than to be told by Great Britain that she will have to discontinue or curtail the import of many agricultural products from the antipodes. So it may well be that the regulating feature in this bill has been embodied with that end in view.
If local boards are to be set up, however, I hope they will not be given the power to control production, because such power in relation to farm products might have disastrous results. I have in mind the condition in my own district and up through the Fraser valley, where to-day more milk is produced than can be sold on the fluid milk market in the larger cities. At one time we had a similar condition in regard to eggs. I should view with alarm any possibility of a local board putting a ring around those areas and telling others: "You cannot come in because to-day we are producing more than we can consume." I think a power like that would be far too drastic. I am sure hon. members from the province of British Columbia will agree on this, that British Columbia fruit and milk men believe that the producers to-day should regulate their own production. I would ask the house to note that in the province of British Columbia neither the fruit men nor the milk producers have so far asked any government to bear any of the expense of helping them to market their products.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. gentleman a question. When he speaks of control does he mean control of production or limitation of production?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
The two terms are practically the -same; if you limit production you are controlling production, but when I made that statement I had in mind the possibility of a local board coming to the conclusion that there were enough growers in a particular area and that no more should be allowed into it, which might limit the further progress of that section of the country and, of course, limit the production of that commodity.
We in the province of British Columbia, in the Fraser valley at least, are not asking for any finacial help, nor have we asked for it from any government. What we ask is that we be given the right to pool all the proceeds in any organization we may set up, and to make levies. In order to make the position clear and to acquaint the house with the conditions existing in that part of the country I think I should take a few moments to give a resume of the largest organization which exists
in the Fraser valley, namely the Fraser Valley Milk Producers' Association. Before going on with that, however, just in passing I should like to refer to a statement that has been made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) both in and out of this house, to the effect thatt he was very glad to see this government adopting planned economy, shall I say, which has been advocated by members in the far corner. Let me tell the hon. gentleman and the members of this house that in British Columbia the farmers were some years ahead of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. Long before that organization was thought of we had this Fraser Valley Milk Producers' Association, and we had the dairy products act put through in 1929, after being proposed in 1928. So we did not have to depend on that group for the suggestion of planned economy; our farmers were progressive enough, shall I say, to get that act put through.
This organization of which I speak was started in 1913, but there was some difficulty in regard to finances and operations were not commenced until 1917. There are three or four plants. One is in Vancouver, which is the headquarters with regard to wholesale milk and creamery products; cottage cheese is made there; there is a storage warehouse and general offices are maintained. Then in the city of Chilliwack, where the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber) resides, they have a utility plant which takes care of butter, cheese, powdered milk, casein and semi-solid butter milk. Then at Abbotsford they have an evaporating milk plant with a capacity of 1,300 cases daily. In 1917 the membership was 848, but by 1932 it had increased to 3,567. The assets, when the company started, amounted to $166,000 in round figures, while to-day they are over $1,000,000. The capital invested at that time totalled $77,000; the present capital is well over $1,000,000. The butter fat handled in 1917 amounted to 1,709,528 pounds, while in 1932 the butter fat handled amounted to 5,724,269 pounds.
Might I point out, Mr. Speaker, that all ihe capital was subscribed by the individual farmers in $50 shares; deferred payments were permitted, at the rate of from one to four cents per pound of butter fat, and if necessary payments were made in stock instead of in cash. Six per cent interest was paid on all paid up capital, but this organization has never received any financial assistance from any government. During the peak of production each year they finance by
Marketing Act-Mr. Reid

means of loans from the bank, the loans being retired as the stocks are reduced. In these years the butter fat handled totals well over 58,000,000 pounds, and the total net value to the farmers concerned has amounted to more than $30,000,000. The average price per pound of butter fat, during the whole period, was 524 cents. I ask hon. members to note particularly what I am about to say, because I think it is very striking indeed; it shows what cooperation can accomplish when farmers get together to market their own product. During the period from 1917 to 1929 the Fraser Valley Milk Producers' Association was able to reduce the spread allowed for fluid milk distribution from 29 cents to 20 cents per gallon; they were able also to raise the value of the fluid milk to the producer by approximately 23 cents per pound of butter fat, without raising the price to the consumer.
I ask the house to take note of that. Not only was the price of butter fat raised; the price of milk to the consumer was not increased during that period. The table I have before me shows the effect of increased prices with regard to increased production, indicating how the law of supply works out if it is not permitted to run wild. The pool value in 1917 was 45 cents per pound of butter fat; the pool value in 1928-1 am taking the years before the act was declared to be ultra vires- was 60 cents per pound, an increase of 33 per cent. The butter fat production increased from 2.000,000 pounds, in round figures, to roughly 6,000,000 pounds, while the price for which butter was sold was 40 cents per pound in 1928, as it was in 1917. The price of fluid milk to the consumer was the same in both years also; it was 11 cents per quart. Not only was the price the same during those years; the quality of the milk was greatly improved, due to the introduction of more modern methods and greater cooperation among the farmers.
Some difficulty was encountered, however, because only fifty per cent of the milk produced in the valley is consumed as fluid milk, the other fifty per cent being manufactured into lower priced products such as ice cream, butter and so forth. With the pooling of the prices when the organization was standing together the average was raised so that it did not matter whether a farmer shipped his milk to the fluid market or to the factory; prices were pooled and there was an equal distribution among all the farmers. Some dissension started, however, and one or two farmers who did not belong to the association were offered higher prices in outside distMr. Reid.]
tributing centres. A rush was made, which placed too much fluid milk on the market at one time, and as a result the price fell very rapidly. Then the farmers went to the provincial government asking that legislation be enacted which would compel the farmers in any area to come into what was known as the pool. Just here let me say, Mr. Speaker, that we have heard a great deal about the marketing act in Great Britain. It might interest the house to know that the act passed in British Columbia in 1929, which later was declared ultra vires, was the act which guided the farmers in Great Britain. My information is that that act was copied in Great Britain. It would seem therefore that we in British Columbia can take a little credit in this instance for being leaders in an organized effort to control and help the dairy and farming industries.
That legislation was put into effect, and it contained provisions which I believe might well be included in the present measure. I hope that the bill before us, 'before becoming law, may include the provisions which were embodied in the legislation of the province of British Columbia-and I have referred to that legislation (because I think it is as good as the British legislation. Under our scheme sixty-six per cent of the people in an area or attending the public meetings could petition the government so as to compel the other people to subscribe to the scheme. That took place in British Columbia, and there was no great difficulty in obtaining the support of the sixty-six per cent who wished to organize. However there were those who viewed with alarm the fact that farmers were being forced to cooperate. Those people did not want to cooperate, but wished to sell their products by themselves at any and at every time. The bill was attacked and ultimately declared ultra vires of the province because the farmers who were shipping outside the province could not be controlled by the provincial legislation. After the case had been considered at law-and it went to the old country for final consideration-the provincial act was declared ultra vires, because the provincial government could not levy on the farmer anything in the nature of indirect taxation. The act directed the committee to levy upon shippers who sold more than their quota an amount sufficient to compensate those who were obliged to take less than their quota in the fluid milk market. This was called the adjustment levy.
I would ask you to note, Mr. Speaker, that the operation of this plan had a wonderful effect on the maintenance of prices,

Marketing Act-Mr. Reid
because if the farmer sold his milk for less than 73 cents per pound butter fat he would have less than his neighbour who did not sell, for the simple reason that the commission assumed that he got at least 73 cents. The commission were also directed to deduct by levy on every pound of fat produced a sum sufficient to take care of administration costs. Both these levies were found by the privy council to be indirect taxes and declared beyond the competency of the legislature to enact. However, during the period between January 1, 1930, and April 30, 1931, when our markets were operating under that legislation, the parties concerned enjoyed the best market for their products they had ever had or have had since. When the influence of the act ceased to function everyone piled on to the higher priced market-the fluid milk market -which was bringing a rate of 73 cents a pound butter fat, with the result that the price was hammered down within six weeks to 33 cents per pound butter fat, and that low price was maintained for about a year. Then, in April, 1933, the price came up slightly, to 45 cents, and ever since has gradually crumbled away until to-day it is less than 40 cents per pound butter fat. The result has been that with the exception of a very small percentage all the people want to be placed in such a position that they shall be obliged to play the game and not be permitted to abuse the market. I understand that the price now prevailing in the valley is from 12 cents to 14 cents per gallon, away below cost of production.
The position of farmers is different from that of industrialists. When the industrialist has a plant which is not paying he immediately closes the doors, with the result that his deficits and operating expenses cease. But the farmer has his home and his stock; his land cannot be neglected, and he has to continue. In that respect the farmers are different from any other class and are forced to carry on even at a loss. During the past few years most of them have been going deeper and deeper into debt. As to just how long they can carry on at from 12 cents to 14 cents per gallon I should not care to hazard a guess.
After this short resume of conditions we have experienced in the Fraser valley I shall direct my remarks to the bill now under consideration. May I say that I believe in some respects it goes too far, and in others not far enough. Some hon. members seem to think that the bill contains provisions enforcing pooling. I believe the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) stated the bill could deal only in generalities. I am of the opinion that pooling 74726-172
is not at present embodied in the bill. We know that this measure includes products of the forest, sea, lake and mine. Under it assistance might be given to many industries which are in no need of artificial aid. The minister may also set up and dissolve a board. I do not think he should have that right. In Tny view the industry should ask for the board. As stipulated in the Dairy Products Sales Adjustment Act of 1929 such boards should be established only on vote of the people. That procedure would be entirely democratic, and if it were adopted one could not suggest a dictatorship if a majority of people in a certain area voted to come within the provisions of this measure. Moreover, when we place the control of exports and imports of natural products in the hands of a board we are going a great distance. I am somewhat afraid of the words which appear in subsection (1) of section 5:
. . . the production and marketing or the production or marketing . . .
I believe marketers alone should not be allowed to set up boards and have control. I do not at this time intend to set up straw men or to cite hypothetical cases, but if marketers alone are allowed to set up local boards I would view with alarm what might happen to the salmon fishing industry of British Columbia, in which instance the product is handled by cannerymen. If a board were set up to take care of the manufactured product it could and might result in measures to the detriment of the fishermen. The same might apply to fruit canning interests. Being apart from the producers it might well develop that the local industry would eventually control the producers.
The clauses in the bill are obscure, and I should like the Minister of Agriculture to take note of the demands made by people in the province of British Columbia who are asking that the provisions as to pooling be made very very clear and definite. Legal authorities in British Columbia have discussed the bill and have made it clear that in their opinion this measure does not at the present time contain pooling clauses. They believe that the federal government should embody in the bill such a provision because that is what the people in the lower Fraser valley are requesting, and also the power to make levies.
I have taken this opportunity to place myself on record, because in my view the bill is very important. I know some hon. members hold the view that marketing is not the

Marketing Act-Mr. Laurin

principle behind the bill. I have endeavoured' to indicate my belief that there is more regulating than marketing in the bill, but I am prepared to give it the benefit of the doubt and vote for its second reading in the hope that when it gets to committee the matters I have discussed will be- taken into consideration and changes made adequately to take care of the representations and demands of the farmers of the Fraser Valley. If these things are not made abundantly clear I shall be forced to vote against the third reading of the bill, but, as I have stated, I am prepared to permit it to go to committee.
Mr. GEORGES P. LAURIN (Jacques Cartier): Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this bill on marketing I am mindful of the fact that I am the representative of the constituency of Jacques Cartier which has a population of over 140,000 people. The population of one of the provinces, Prince Edward Island, is only 88,000 people, so I think it must be admitted that the constituency of Jacques Cartier has some right to consideration in this House of Commons. That constituency is made up of all the elements which go to make up our fair dominion. We have the humble labourer, the descendant of many Canadian generations. We have the farmer who has inherited his farm from 'his ancestral fathers. We have the immigrant who came from Great Britain or middle or southern Europe who has established himself end has accepted Canada as his only home. We have manufacturers, both large and small, and we have traders, bankers, capitalists and a railway leader. But in discussing this bill I must not forget that the majority of my constituents are consumers like those in the constituency of the hon. member for North Timiskaming (Mr. Bradette). My constituency is on the island of Montreal and my constituents are made up of French and English speaking Canadians. They are both consumers and producers, and contrary to the expressed opinion of the hon. member for North Timiskaming, I am in favour of the bill. I believe that it represents a step toward the fulfilment of the wishes of both the consumer and the producer.
I believe in due course of time the operations of this legislation will result in a fairer spread between the consumer and the producer. The profits derived from the marketing of our rich natural resources will be more equitable and there will be ensured to the manufacturer, to the trader and to the consumer that sound equilibrium which can come only from regulated markets. Agriculture will obtain a fair return for its investment and

labour while the consumer will be able to purchase at a price commensurate with the wages he receives. The farmer producer and the labourer consumer will both receive fair treatment and there will be a continuous and steady market for the products of the manufacturer. The agricultural producer will be assured of a home market for his products while the wage earner will be able to give to the agricultural producer a fair return for his product. The returns received by both the producer and the consumer will be sufficient to ensure the manufacturer a steady market for his product. The profits which the manufacturer receives may be somewhat lower but his market will be steady. An equilibrium will be preserved among our principal industries, agriculture, manufacturing and labour. These industries will still be capable of acting for themselves for their own common good, but the fact remains that they must of necessity depend upon one another.
Because of our affinity with England and our proximity to the United States we had hopes that one day-this applies particularly to the province of Quebec-we might emulate the great industrial activities of England and the New England States. At one time England admittedly held the premier place in the manufacturing world. It developed its manufacturing, its commercial and trading activities to an immense degree but it crushed every effort brought forward to protect and secure a market for its agricultural industry. This was done in order that the salaries of the wage earners should be kept at a point where the profits of the manufacturer and the trader would be enhanced. But in time its outside manufacturing outjets became gradually decreased and it then realized the necessity of organizing its agricultural and labour consuming population. This necessity formed the basic reason for the establishing of the British marketing board. Here in Canada we have also allowed our agriculture to decline. This has happened in the west but more particularly in the province of Quebec.
If this were simply my own opinion, I would willingly allow hon. members opposite from Quebec to challenge my declaration, but this opinion has been advanced by one who played a very important part in the direction of our provincial affairs between 1920 and 1930. The Minister of Roads, one of the most important portfolios in the province of Quebec, had obtained for his department a vote of $17,500,000 for the construction of roads in that province. He had however the courage to resign that portfolio and to accept instead that of agriculture. A staunch Liberal, he did

Marketing Act*-Mr. Laurin
not shirk from denying the compliments which Mr. Taschereau had been continuously showering upon our farmers, on the eve of every election, and he disregarded the flowery speeches of his colleagues. In his first speech as Minister of Agriculture in 1926, at Sherbrooke, and I believe the hon. member for Sherbrooke will admit it, the Hon. L. Perron- for it is he of whom I speak-declared:
Notre agriculture est dans le marasme.
That is to say, our agriculture is in a state of atrophy. I would add, it appears to be in a bog, sinking at the slightest effort, and drastic means must be taken to save it. Unhappily Mr. Perron died. His successor is a most capable man, but his efforts, encouraged one day by Mr. Taschereau, are thwarted the day following. We saw Mr. Taschereau pass a bill to cooperate with the present government in its efforts to alleviate the state of agriculture. But on Tuesday, April 24, 1934, he comes forward with the assertion that this marketing board will infringe upon provincial rights as regards agriculture, and he declares his strict opposition to this bill. Mr. Taschereau is not only a past master in politics; he is also a noted lawyer. He should know better therefore than to try to incite the people of our province to mistakes-he has done it so often to their detriment. Had he read Hansard he would have received a legal lesson from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) who, speaking on this bill, drew the attention of the house to section 95 of the British North America Act, which reads:
In each province the legislature may make laws in relation to agriculture in the province, and to immigration into the province; and it is hereby declared that the parliament of Canada may from time to time make laws in relation to agriculture in any or all of the provinces, and to immigration into any or all of the provinces;
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre directed attention particularly to the following provision in this section:

So it would' seem to a layman at least that we need not worry too much with regard to the difficulty of jurisdiction if this dominion parliament acts in the matter.

Without permitting wide discretionary authority to the individuals chosen to administer and execute the laws, and without reserving to them ample power to give, and to compel obedience to orders, it would be impossible for the business of government in the state to be carried on.

Mr. Speaker, this debate has covered a wide range of arguments both for and against the principle of the bill. I therefore do not intend to detain the 'house very long, because I doubt very much whether I could refer to anything particularly new in connection with the matter. The bill of course is drawn in somewhat general terms, and consequently lends itself to a wide scope of imagination on the part of hon. members. I have gone over quite a number of the speeches delivered, and the arguments advanced by some would remind one of the mythological story of Pandora's box which was supposed to contain all the ills that flesh is heir to, while others regard it as full of all the blessings that can come to humanity. The bill, however, is an experiment and necessarily so. We are actually trying something that is new and we must do so because we are living under new conditions. Therefore, if it is possible for critics to sit down and point to this, that and the other danger, I am not surprised, because, no matter how much care is exercised, we cannot get away from danger and the possibility of error. How much more, then, is it possible to say that dangers may arise when we are trying to do something that is new? Everything new in the world has been attacked by somebody-new proposals, new discoveries, the good and the bad, have been laughed at.
A good deal of time has been taken up in the house in arguing about just how much evil this board could do if it really wanted to do that. There is no question about it because if you give any individual or board power to do good you cannot separate from that the power to do evil. Every human

Marketing Act-Mr. Kennedy (Peace River)
being, every human agency has a potential devil as well as a potential angel and we cannot entirely avoid either in anything we try to do. So I am not at all surprised that certain dangers have been pointed out as possibilities arising from the setting up of this board.
There is need for something of this kind. Producers in various lines throughout the length and breadth of Canada have tried to build up their own cooperative organizations and have succeeded in doing some measure of good, but I do not believe there is in this country to-day a cooperative organization that believes it has or really can get control of the marketing situation without some government assistance. I do not know of any such organization. Cooperative organizations in the last ten years have had their ups and downs. I know hardly any cooperative organization that has been functioning with any measure of success, that intends to go back on cooperation and that is not asking for some further control of marketing conditions in the interest of the producers.
I intend to confine my argument and my illustrations to the subject of live stock, because I am more familiar with the conditions pertaining thereto than with those affecting any of the other commodities that may be handled by boards set up in accordance with the provisions of this legislation and working in cooperation with the provinces and cooperative organizations. In 1931 we had a peculiar situation in Canada; one of the cooperatives had a contract to ship cattle to a cooperative in the old land and was doing well, building up reserves until Britain abandoned the gold standard. Then the change in the value of British currency and the drop in prices relative to all prices in this country at once put the export cattle business of the dominion in jeopardy, because there was no way to protect shippers exporting to the old country from the loss arising out of the difference in exchange. I believe if we had had then a board somewhat along the lines of the board now proposed to be set up we might have adjusted tbajt loss, on the small percentage of our cattle being exported, on the basis of the cattle industry itself carrying the burden, thus preventing the ruinous decline of prices that followed and has continued up to 1933.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) suggested that this measure was evidence of the fact that parliament is losing control over the executive. But parliament
at any session can repeal the act founded upon this bill if it wants to; it can abolish the whole thing, so surely we have parliamentary control. But throughout the whole of his speech, extending over a period of two hours, he did not have a word to say about the plight in which the farmers find themselves due to the very low prices that prevail for their products. The right hon. gentleman said a great deal about liberty. What about liberty? A policeman on the street corner regulating traffic is interfering with liberty, but he is preserving more liberty than he is destroying. The leader of the opposition calls attention to the fact that certain rights were wrested from the crown years ago when the Magna Charta was secured. Then he goes on to say that he is not an advocate of laissez-faire, and points to certain bills passed by Liberals regulating and controlling industry and various groups within industry. The rest of his argument seems to be to the effect that bills passed to regulate industry by other parties should be thrown into the discard or killed. If it was a sound principle in the last century to regulate hours of labour and wages and working conditions, it is just as sound to tackle the problem confronting us to-day, which are creating just as great difficulties for the farmers as were experienced in connection with workers in factories in the centuries past.
The hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) the ex-Minister of Agriculture, is supporting the principle of this bill, and I am not surprised that he should do so. He had the responsibility when in office of administering the legislation and organization for the control and elimination of bovine tuberculosis and the maintenance and improvement of the health of live stock generally. Every time you have a government organization coming into the picture there is the possibility of coercion of some individuals. Was there no coercion of individuals in connection with the enforcement of health regulations in regard to live stock? Certainly there was, and there were mistakes made. But I submit that because the government came into the picture we made progress in the matter of health of live stock and a healthful food supply for the people of Canada and the people to whom we export our products, and this could not have been accomplished had it been left to individual farmers throughout the length and breadth of the country. The same thing is true in connection with hogs and the control of hog cholera. I submit that individuals cannot do for themselves what governments can do for
2720	COMMONS
Marketing Act-Mr. Kennedy (Peace River)
them. It is true that there are some things that can best be left to the individual, but it is also true that the best progress has been made through cooperation, between individuals organized in cooperative associations, and between these organizations and governments, provincial and federal. I believe that marketing conditions in Canada and throughout the world, especially in connection with live stock, make it necessary to-day that governments should assist in that problem. How can individual farmers in Saskatchewan or Manitoba or the Peace River country, handling a few head of live stock, keep abreast of the necessary knowledge concerning quota regulations, tariffs, shipping and market conditions in the various markets of Canada as well as of Great Britain? How can individuals and organizations, without some coordinating body, pick and choose and control the sending of the right type of product to Great Britain and decide upon the right type to keep in Canada and send to the various home markets? In order to do that it is necessary to be able to measure the demand. It requires statistical information that individuals have not the time or the facilities to obtain; other information is required as to health conditions and so on. I submit that with a board of the kind proposed there are possibilities of efficient handling and marketing of our live stock, with a guarantee of quality and consequent protection of the name of Canada in connection with its exports to the British market that would not be possible under any other arrangement.
