I would like to give a few illustrations that come to my mind as to what "rugged individualism" means in connection with marketing, showing why it is a good thing to limit the right of individuals to do what they like. Years ago there was a very good crop of potatoes in Scotland. The price was very low. But when spring came there was a demand for potatoes in New York; some shipments were going forward, and the price improved. Then a Glasgow dealer with more desire for profit than conscience sent over a load of bad potatoes and ruined the market. Would it have been a good thing for Scotland if there had been a board watching the kind of potatoes that went out, with the right to say to this man; "You cannot send these bad potatoes out of the country"? Yet that would be an interference with his liberty. A few years ago in northern Alberta we had some experience 
with marketing turkeys on the Pacific coast through a government organization. There was what we thought an orderly market, in turkeys going forward in a reasonable flow. Those in charge of the shipments had knowledge of what the market would take and were feeding it, providing enough to meet the demand at reasonable prices. A few others who were interested in shipping turkeys, without any attempt to keep in touch with the conditions, sent out a few extra loads, more than the market would absorb, and the result was they not only took a loss themselves but broke the price generally. It was not good for the producer; it was not good for the consumers, because it certainly interfered with the supply of turkeys from northern Alberta in future years.
I do not believe that this argument about the consumer is well taken. You cannot build a civilization on either producers or consumers alone; you have to consider both. When someone says: "Oh the producers are getting too much; we have got to look at this from the standpoint of the consumer," it seems to me like saying; Here is a man with only one good left leg; all we need is another man with a good right leg. Rather we should say; "We will have a man with two legs, both sound." And so we seek a civilization with two sound legs, represented by producers and consumers. What a body of this kind should aim at is not low prices to the consumers or high prices to the producers, but knowledge of what is a reasonable cost of efficient production, and then see to it that both parties to the bargain get fair treatment. Any other approach to the question of marketing is in my judgment entirely wrong.
It has been said that in this bill the minister is asking for very wide powers. But I would rather ask for powers a little wider than necessary than not wide enough. We Shall have to trust someone to use ordinary common sense in connection with the application of this act to industry. It has been said that we should do exactly as they do in Britain. But Britain is a small country, about the size of my constituency, and there are 244 other constituencies. Britain is a country with stability in practically all lines of production, going on from year to year and from generation to generation, while we have tremendous fluctuations in our production, with changes as between district and district and province and province from year to year. It has been said that we should refer every scheme to parliament, but it has been pointed out also that the British parliament sits about twelve months of

Marketing Act-Mr. Bourgeois
the year while we sit only part of the year, and we have ten parliaments instead of one. It is an entirely different thing, and I want to say that we have to try this measure on the basis of trial and error, if you like, using our best judgment as we proceed and learning by experience as we go along. I believe there are sections in the bill that may be amended in committee, but control through a body set up by the central government, cooperating with the provinces and the producers' organizations, is an absolute essential in practically every line of marketing of which I have knowledge.
The hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Yallance) read into the record two letters which he received, and while in his argument he did not endorse the sentiments they contained they created the impression that the cooperatives of the old country were very much opposed to policies of this sort because we were trying to raise prices to the agriculturists. The hon. member referred to two letters that appeared in the Glasgow Herald, I believe. I think anyone who has sufficient knowledge of the subject to express an opinion must know that agricultural prices must come up; if they do not we had better get ready for wholesale 'bankruptcy and repudiation, because there can be no avoiding it. Agricultural prices have to come up at least to the point where they will pay the cost of efficient production, or we must face the alternative. But I do not think it is true to say that even the Scottish cooperative does not realize that prices of wheat are too low. The Scottish cooperative had some experience in connection with wheat in Saskatchewan, and they went out of business some years ago. I do not think people who have had an experience of that kind would be expected to think wheat prices should not be raised, as well as the prices of other agricultural products. I obtained from the library of the Department of Agricuture the People's Year Book, the 17th annual of the English and Scottish cooperative wholesale societies, 1934. Under the heading " Prices and Debtors" here is what I found:
The farmers, and other producers of raw materials and what are called "primary" articles, have been ruined by the fall in their prices because they habitually work with borrowed money, borrowed on contracts made long ago. So the farmer found that in order to pay interest on his debts, he had to sell twice or three times as much wheat as would have met the charge, if the wheat could be sold at the price current when the debt was contracted. In other words, the fall in prices has undermined the solvency of debtors and made debt contracts inequitable, owing to the change in the value of money since they were
first entered into. Unless prices can be restored to, and maintained at, a level that will enable debtors to meet their liabilities, a general bankruptcy and scaling down of debts was inevitable. This was especially so in America, where during the boom years debts had been contracted on an enormous scale; and so there was a good deal of justification for President Roosevelt, when he decided that the first and most important thing for him to do was to force prices up, and that the restoration of the gold standard' might, as far as America was concerned, wait for a better opportunity.
There we have the clear statement that the Scottish cooperative believes the prices of primary products must be raised, so in setting up a board of this kind I do not think we need fear any danger from that source at all. I wish therefore, Mr. Speaker, to repeat that I support the principle of the bill and congratulate the minister on his attempt to bring something of this kind into effect.

It is not
my intention to enter into the minute details

Marketing Act-Mr. Bourgeois
of this bill; others, possessing a wider experience, I frankly admit, have done so. The hon. Minister of Agriculture, numerous members on your right, sir, and some on the extreme left, have enumerated and set forth the benefits which we will derive from this measure.
It meets with opposition, much opposition, and our opponents not only have raised against its adoption all the objections that their imagination could bring to bear, but it also gave them the pretext to launch against the government an unrelenting attack which had its inception not so much because of the deficiencies in the bill as in the well known habit that our friends have developed of criticizing all measures emanating from this side of the house. However, this was to be expected and there is reason to note once more the inherent weakness of our parliamentary regime which causes certain minds to look upon and discuss questions from the strict viewpoint of their narrow political party interests rather than consider them on their merit and, in the present instance, with the idea of finding the most suitable remedy to the present situation which we all deplore.
Many economists have sought the causes of the present crisis; they have found that they are numerous: the world war, frantic overproduction and unrestrained stock speculations. However, it is not sufficient to limit ourselves to inquiry into the causes only and to confine ourselves simply to an academical discussion, what is of the utmost importance is to endeavour to accomplish something, apply the remedies. Heads of nations have recognized that this was an urgent duty. Hitler in Germany; Mussolini in Italy; Roosevelt in the neighbouring republic, have all maintained in their various respective experiments, that they had found the solution to the disheartening problem.
This is not the time to criticize the experiments tried out in other countries. What is important, however, to note-and I wish to draw the attention of the house on this particular point-is the tendency of governments to intervene in the free action of personal endeavours in order to regulate, concentrate them and thereby make them produce greater results, or what is better, results that they could not produce without such intervention.
But, the cry is raised: It is state monopoly, it is an encroachment on the rights of parliament, an attempt against our parliamentary regime and a step towards oligarchy which would suppress, in favour of a few, the authority that parliament must, by virtue of our constitution, possess over the affairs of our country!

The most bitter criticism is, especially directed against these so-called exorbitant powers granted to the governor in council, in the marketing board act. This criticism is, to my mind, most unreasonable. There is no cause for such fears, it is neither a question of state monopoly, such as Plato conceived it in his treatises "The Republic" and "The Laws," or of land nationalization advocated by Henry George. It is a bold measure, I admit, but necessary, the special character of which is justified by the exceptional grave circumstances in which we are situated at present.

speechtext:
Since
Louis Hebert established on the Canadian soil of New France the first farm, up to the settling of the Canadian west, numerous generations of farmers, in ploughing and seeding the land, succeeded in making a livelihood for themselves and their families. No one will truly contend that our soil has since become sterile. Whence comes this depression in farming? How does it happen that our farmers, toiling with the same steadfastness and energy, as in the past, on our lands, have, owing to the low prices of farm products, great difficulty in earning a livelihood, so much so that they can say with the "Chemineau" of Richepin:
Je songe aux bles coupes qui ne sont pas les notres
Et dont les epis murs font du pain pour les autres.
If closely examined we find that it is not, in this instance, so much a question of production as distribution. The establishing of co-operative societies in this country gave rise to great hopes which, unfortunately, were only partly realized. The reason is-as the hon. Minister of Agriculture pointed out-that these co-operative associations did not receive the help to which they were entitled, they were unable to organize on a stable financial basis, they had to meet a disloyal competition by certain corporations which were interested in seeing them disappear and they were also too busy marketing their products without giving a thought to quality and, I shall add,, to labelling and packing. Darwin put forth the famous theory of "the survival of the fittest." I am not called upon to express an opinion on this theory from the view-point of natural sciences; however, it seems to me unquestionable that it is an undoubted maxim as regards natural products and their exportation.
Whether it is a question of local, national or world market, it is the best product which not

Marketing Act-Mr. Bourgeois
only obtains the highest price, but has a better chance of finding a purchaser. That is the first object which is sought by the bill under consideration.
Secondly, it is important, that such a product be packed before being marketed, so as to make it as attractive as possible, regardless of its excellence, because, no matter what its quality may be, it will not find a purchaser, if, on the market, there is a foreign product superior to it in this respect. Moreover, it is necessary that it should be well labelled, the label should indicate the place where made and thus ensuring the best and most convincing advertisement.
If the present act which creates a marketing board, the subsidiary boards could bring about these three results, I think that there would be reason to be amply satisfied.
I do not contend that this bill-nor does the hon. Minister of Agriculture do so, as he plainly stated-is on all points perfect; however, to my mind, it is a loyal, sincere and excellent endeavour made to protect the farmer as much as the manufacturer.
Every farmer, in my constituency, that I consulted on the subject-and I had occasion to talk with a large number of them-look upon this measure favourably and they have expressed their faith in its efficiency. Mr. Albert Rioux, President of "L'Union catholique des cultivateurs" approved of it. Mr. J-S. Royier, President of the Canned Fruit and Vegetable Association, also approved of it.
While Mr. Oscar Gatineau in the "Bulletin des Agriculteurs" in its issue of April 5 last, expresses himself as follows:
No doubt, it is a real extraordinary scheme, a new departure. Some fear that the scheme may lead us too far while others think that the government assumes too much power.
We do not believe that any one can even imagine that the government intends to create a board' detrimental to the farming class. Of all the governments we have had, at Ottawa, the Bennett government is the one which has shown the greatest readiness to help the farmers. Before contending that too much assistance has been given to farmers, there remains a long way to go. Let us not be anxious about others, they are somewhat there to champion their cause.
Mr. Bennett is not afraid to shoulder responsibilities, he has no hesitation in having the necessary powers turned over to him and he is not afraid to resort to whatever means are necessary to remedy the evils from which we suffer.
The farmers have therefore reason to rejoice in this bill which is being enacted for them and from which there is reason to expect much. What Mr. Bennett has done hitherto for the farming class warrants us to repose confidence in him for what he undertakes.
I do not wish to close my remarks without mentioning the fact that Mr. Robert Ryan, one of the most prominent liberals of Three Rivers and the leader of the Municipal Council of that city, has entirely approved of this bill. In a letter which he forwarded to the right hon. Prime Minister on April 13, 1934, Mr. Ryan enclosed a short essay dealing with the question under consideration and expresses himself as follows:
(Text). I believe the creation of the marketing board is a move in the right direction. On page 2, paragraph 4, in my brief, you will notice I made reference to a Co-operative Sales Corporation for the handling of farm products for exports. The marketing board is another, and perhaps a better method of accomplishing the same purpose.
In the above mentioned essay, he made the following judicial remarks.
I am a firm believer that the farmers of each province should produce all the farm products, for which there is a local demand, and for which the soil and climate are suitable. Products for export should be handled by a Co-operative Sales Corporation. These products, should be put up under a uniform trade mark with the name of the province stamped on each package or container. All produce should be graded and packed according to the instructions of the Sales Corporation.
The time has arrived for planned and not lopsided development, if we want Canada to be developed for the benefit of all its inhabitants, a more balanced rural population compared' to the population of the cities and a proper balance between agricultural and industrial production and prices.
A success can only be made of farming when the farmer is decided and follows proper direction. A success can only be made of selling farm produce when the merchants and consumers are convinced that they should purchase such produce on account of quality, regular supply and good service. Therefore, the education of the farmer, merchant and' consumer is absolutely necessary.
What is wanted is organization and leadership in centres that should be selected by the government, as points that should be developed for the collection, processing and distribution of farm products.
In this same essay Mr. Ryan, whose suggestions I entirely agree with, pointed out to the government the opportunity of subsidizing the growing of beets and this, especially, in the Three Rivers district.
In that locality and within a radius of 50 miles the soil is most favourable to the growth of this vegetable.
And he quoted in this respect a resolution adopted on April 1, 1922, by the Committee on Agriculture and Colonization, the resolution contained the following recommendation:
Your committee further recommends that, if no successful attempt be made in the immediate
Marketing Act-Mr. Bourassa

future by the refineries to increase the facilities for the manufacture of beet sugar, the government should take into consideration steps to accomplish that end.
I hope-may I casually say so-that the government will find the means to put into practice these suggestions, for it would be an excellent means of increasing the wealth of this country and thereby reduce unemployment in that section.
I shall close my remarks by pointing out that the object of this bill is an excellent one; that if, in principle, the state must abstain to invade the personal activities of citizens, for fear of paralyzing them, there are situations- and the present is one of them-which necessitate the intervention of the state; that this bill owing to its provisions constitutes a sound measure necessitated by the critical circumstances in which we find ourselves and it behooves all members of this house to set aside all party lines and give it their entire approval.

Mr. Speaker, unable as I was, on account of illness, to follow the debate very closely, I have read most of the speeches which have been delivered in support of or in opposition to this measure. However, it was some time before I could arrive at a decision on the matter, because so many good arguments have been put forward on both sides. I should like to sum up as briefly as possible the decision at which I have arrived.
A olear distinction must be made between the object of the bill and parliamentary procedure. It may be because of my old habits as a British parliamentarian, but I think there is some reason for keeping close to parliamentary tradition. At the present stage, all that is before us is the object of the bill as expressed in the preamble and the title. This measure purports "to improve the methods and practices involved in the marketing of natural products in Canada and in export trade, and to make further provision in connection therewith." I think I can safely say that, perhaps with the exception of a few ghosts haunting the ruins of Liberal economics, practically the whole house is committed to the principle of this bill. In fact, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), who was most effective in several parts of his speech, indicated that he was in favour of some measure to control the marketing of produce, both inside and outside of Canada. In the manner in which he made that statement he practically admitted the desirability of passing legislation to deal with marketing.

Therefore, it seems to me that the only logical position is that taken by the right hon. gentleman himself on the relief and central bank bills. In connection with both those measures he expressed strong views; he invoked the same arguments as he did against this measure, that they were against the spirit if not the letter of the constitution, that they meant the abdication of the rights of parliament to an irresponsible body or to the executive, as far as the spending of money under the relief act was concerned. However, he voted for the second reading of these bills, reserving to himself the right to oppose them in committee or on third reading if they were not amended according to his views. I followed his example in those two instances. When I spoke quite suddenly on the central bank bill it was to oppose the amendment proposed by my hon. friend to my left. I take the same ground now. Being in favour of some measure to deal with the marketing of produce, I am not opposed to the second reading of the bill.
As regards the measure itself I do not propose to follow the unparliamentary example given by most speakers and enter into a close analysis of all the clauses of the bill. That is the work of the committee after the bill has passed its present stage. But the preamble and title of the bill are not comprehensive enough to justify our voting for or against the second reading without entering into a consideration of at least the main features of the bill. In this connection my opinion comes closer to that of the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) than *to any other opinion expressed in the house. I read his speech very carefully and I am pleased to repeat now what I told him in private, that it is the best speech I have heard from him since I came back to this house.

speechtext:
Yes, it is saying a great deal. His speech contained as much wit as any of his others, and perhaps was a little more serious.
The bill contains some provisions which are good or which may produce good. It contains other provisions which may produce good or bad results according to the manner in which the law may be administered, but that may be said of almost all legislation. It contains other provisions which in my humble opinion are decidedly bad.
I shall not deal at any length with the constitutional aspect, although there are two features of the bill which could be considered

Marketing Act-Mr. Bourassa
from that angle. First, there is the one raised by the leader of the opposition, a serious one, of the possible conflict of jurisdiction between this parliament and the provincial legislatures. We come up against that obstacle at every session, and I am afraid the more we have to do with economic and social problems, the more that conflict will be increased. The time will come when, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) stated so forcibly some weeks ago, the constitution shall have to be revised, in agreement with the provinces. But I shall not deal with that aspect now.
There is a further constitutional issue, the contempt with which the government-I am using the words of the leader of the opposition-treats parliament and parliamentary institutions. Of course, there is some truth in that, 'but no party in this house has the right to throw stones at their opponents. The Liberal government put this country into war in 1899 by an order in council. That was certainly a far deeper breach of the spirit of the constitution than anything I ever heard of until 1914, when the Conservative administration repeated the same crime with the unanimous approval of the Liberal party. Then again, in 1916, when both parties agreed to prolong parliament beyond its constitutional term, thereby preventing the people to pass judgment on their war policy. That action received unanimous approval with the exception of the hon. member for Nicolet, who resigned. That parliament is now defunct and I can repeat what was then said outside the house: through an infamous pact between the two parties, it prolonged its own life for one year, in utter disregard of the people, in order to plunge Canada more deeply into the abyss of war out of which we have not yet emerged. Surely, at that time, some of the tenets of Liberalism were violated far more deeply than they are by this bill. However, I shall not insist on that at the present time.
The only analysis which I wish to make of the bill is to attempt to foresee the possible operations of the central board and the local boards. As regards the central board to be created by the government, no doubt the leader of the opposition is right when he says that it is practically an abdication on the part of parliament, and even of the executive, a surrender of its powers into the hands of a body very distantly responsible to parliament. But this is only a further step in the direction which parliament has followed for many years, unavoidably in many instances, but perhaps avoidably in others. Some weeks ago, in reference to another matter, I reminded
the house that when this parliament created the audit ofBce it abdicated one of its essential functions. It handed over certain powers to a permanent official, nominated by the government and practically independent of the authority of the Commons, inasmuch as he must be impeached by both houses of parliament. In that instance parliament handed over to that official one of its essential functions, namely, the control of its own expenditures. Yet that was considered an extremely wise measure of reform; and on the whole, I think, it has worked for the good of Canada and of this parliament. When the house handed over to the tribunals of the country, to judges irresponsible to the people and to parliament, the power to decide whether in certain circumstances a member of parliament had been properly elected or not, that was again an abdication of an essential function of parliament, which is to control itself and the qualifications of its members. But let us come nearer to our own day. The creation of the railway commission, one of the best administrative acts of the Liberal government headed by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, was the abdication of a parliamentary function into the hands of an outside body. The creation of the Canadian National corporation was a further abdication of the authority of parliament; so was the creation of the wheat board and of the tariff board as well.
In these days of complicated problems precipitating themselves upon the attention of parliament and of the various classes of our people, and upon the attention of the nation at large, in Canada as in all other countries, the action of parliament would be paralyzed if parliament pretended to deal with all such problems as the parliaments of old dealt with theirs. The world has become mechanized; it has become extremely complicated in matters of trade, finance and so forth; and it requires constant attention, study and the effective work of technicians to cope with all the problems that present themselves. Now, admittedly parliament is unable to do that work; governments are unable to do it; and regretful as it may be to old parliamentarians like the leader of the opposition and myself, attached as we are to those time honoured principles of political liberty, we must recognize that facts are stronger than theories and that we must abide by the necessities of our time. Nevertheless I think that the leader of the opposition and all those who have spoken against this legislation have done their duty
Marketing Act-Mr. Bourassa

and rendered a service to the country in pointing out the dangers in this bill. My friends on the opposite side condemn them for their lack of patriotism because they do not rise above the level of party spirit. Well, I have heard that story from government supporters for the last fifty years; and reading through my parliamentary history of Canada and of England, I find that ministerial supporters have always seen in opposition members a lack of principle, while opposition members have had the same opinion of government supporters. And I suppose that both are equally right and wrong.
It is the duty of an opposition, I will not say to oppose everything, but to criticize; and in order to awaken public opinion they must criticize strongly. It is not the business of the opposition to pass over the defects of ministerial measures. In that regard therefore I would go a little further than the hon. member for Melville. The hon. gentleman balances things. He indicated six good points in the bill, but he did not enumerate the evil points, though he expressed himself quite clearly with regard to some of them. I will not enter into details, but I will state my objections as briefly as possible.
The creation of the central board is I think a necessity in order to cope with such conditions as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) has so ably pointed out, such conditions as exist now in every producing and consuming country, in every importing and exporting country with which we deal at present or with which we may deal in the future. To meet those conditions we must create an economic machinery capable of dealing with the means which those countries have at their disposal. All those countries, whether fascistic, communistic, liberal in the broad sense of the word, or conservative-even old England is moving fast in this direction-are creating machinery to control production, distribution, imports and exports. Even if we adopt the broader policy in trading, which is so ably advocated at each session by the opposition, a policy with which I sympathize much more than I do with the ultraprotective policy of the Conservatives-even if the Liberals came into power and succeeded in getting other countries to purchase more of our goods, selling more of their goods to us-the Liberals would need to have in their hands such legislation as would provide an economic machinery capable of dealing with other countries with their own weapons.
All the countries of Europe have some form of organization similar to that which is con-

templated in the first part of this bill, and I think that we are bound to arm ourselves in the same manner. But where my objections are so strong that I will certainly vote against the third reading of the bill if it is not amended, is with respect to all that deals with the organization of local boards. Perhaps in this I am not expressing the views of many on this side of the house, but I must say that I dread much more the tyranny and abuses of power on the part of the local boards than of the central board. The central board will have to deal with the large issues. They will have to follow the trend of trade all the world over in order to find out, as was so well pointed out to-night by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy), what the requirements of foreign countries will be, not next year or ten years hence but this year-what this country will purchase of our apples, what that country is prepared to purchase of our wheat, what the other country will purchase of live stock or meat products, and so on. No local board can do that, nor can any individual. That is a truism, as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) knows. No individual, no small group of farmers anywhere can do that. Therefore that board must be on the alert and be prepared to inform all producers and exporters throughout the country of the conditions of the market, what produce they should prepare this year for export to this, that and the other country. So far as that is concerned, the creation of the federal board is essential and it must be created as soon as possible; it must set to work from morning to night every day of the week and every week of the month. I repeat: No committee of parliament and no executive power can do that.
But when we come to the question of local boards, I have read with much interest the speech of the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Butcher) who, of course, knows of conditions in England and thus is enabled to enlighten the house as to the defects in this bill. The hon. member for Peace River attempted this evening to answer him by again pointing out something which is very true-the difference in conditions between England and Canada. Of course we admit that, but that does not answer two of the contentions of the hon. member for Last Mountain. There is, first, the danger of creating a small bo<?y of men in each locality, in each county, and numerous bodies in each province who, for their own individual or collective interest, may tyrannize over the other producers in the same locality or the same county or, if they arrive at an under-

Marketing Act-Mr. Bourassa
standing with similar bodies in their region, may tyrannize over the whole region, the whole province and eventually the whole country. Therefore, precisely because of the difference in conditions between Canada and England and because of the difficulty a central board will have of knowing what is really going on in each locality, we may within a short time find ourselves faced with a situation that will be very detrimental to a large proportion of the producers; whether it be a majority or a minority, does not matter very much. In that respect I do not follow the hon. member for Last Mountain. I have no more faith in the infallibility of majorities than in that of minorities. Parties in the minority should not insist too much on the infallibility of majorities. As Montesquieu said once, it would be better in tribunals and parliaments generally to give the award or judgment according to the minority, because the minority is generally in the right and the majority generally in the wrong. That is the condition I dread; I dread it for a large proportion of the producers, farmers, small industrialists, who may directly or indirectly be affected by the operations of this legislation. I dread it most of all for the consumers. The hon. member for Peace River said very properly that producers and consumers are not essentially inimical to one another and that, in a body properly constituted, consumers and producers should act as the two legs under the same body. But I am afraid that this legislation has a tendency to set apart the two legs and to split the body in two. As a matter of fact, the consumer is not even mentioned in this bill; there is no proviso whatever to protect him. Let us not forget, if it is true that the body of the producers and the body of the consumers must not be raised in enmity against each other, consumers to a certain extent are producers and all producers are consumers of other goods which they do not produce. If this legislation is to work for the benefit of all, some great changes will have to be made in order to protect people-whether they be a minority or a majority, I repeat, does not matter-who will not agree to any scheme proposed by any five or ten individuals in any locality, against the tyranny or misrepresentation of the body framing the scheme and sending it to Ottawa to be approved.
The board or the minister will of necessity be subjected to all sorts of influences. We must take men and things as they are in our country as elsewhere, perhaps more so in ours than in many other countries. Political influences will be at work. In constituencies
represented by members supporting the government, you will see that schemes will be accepted much more readily if they are recommended either directly by the member or through his friends on those local boards. That will be the case whether my friends to the right or my friends to the left are in power. I have had experience of parties for forty years: the party spirit is the same in every party. Suppose my hon. friends to the extreme left were to come to power and acquire the qualities and defects of the other parties, the same situation would arise. Human nature is always the same.

No; do not pose as the Pharisee. It may be said: Then nothing should be done. No; we cannot remain paralysed because of the danger of party spirit or local tyranny. But I insist very strongly on the necessity of incorporating in this legislation proper safeguards, first, against that disposition of a few individuals to control the affairs of their locality, of their region, to their own interest, to the interest of those who would be associated with them, disregarding that of others; and, second, more especially to protect the consumers in all classes of the community and in all parts of the dominion. That is entirely apart from the necessity so ably pointed out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. His argument applies mainly to foreign trade, and, in that respect, the attitude of the government is in my opinion incontrovertible. Their position is not one of taste; it is one of necessity. They would be remiss in their duty if they did not now cope energetically with this aspect of the problem, dealing with it with a strong hand and creating as powerful a body as they can to handle the situation. But internally the matter is entirely different; internally the views of the leader of the opposition still have great force. Of course you cannot pass legislation controlling any activity without interfering in some degree with individual liberty. But if we want to live under such conditions as we have come to love and as for generations past we have benefited by, not only in this but in the various countries of our origin, we must not interfere with individual liberty beyond the absolutely essential point. This legislation opens the way to all sorts of interferences with the liberty of the farmer, the gardener, the fruit grower, the dairyman, etc., and the consumer.
Marketing Act-Mr. Bourassa

There is one argument made by the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) which I think has to be considered very seriously as regards internal business. He said the important thing was not so much the control of quantity as of quality. As regards foreign trade I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce has shown in a manner that cannot be disputed that we must control quantity as well as quality with regard to exports and imports. But as regards the exchange of goods between one county and another in the same province, or between different provinces, if you put in the hands of a few individuals in each locality the power to control all the local activities, the shipping of goods to this town and that and the other from east to west, from west to east, I am afraid you will complicate the economic machinery to a much greater extent than you will serve the interests of the various classes.
With these remarks I think I have made it quite clear that in vofing for the second reading I am not committing mj'self to the support of the legislation, but simply following the example of the leader of the opposition as regards the central bank and the relief act, in fact following the traditions of parliament. I support the purport of this bill; I may oppose most of its provisions.
Before closing I would like to pass a remark for the benefit of my friends of the province of Quebec, especially my good Conservative friends from that province, and even some of my Liberal friends. For the last six months some of them have been very busy depicting the group to the left here as something akin to the bolshevists of Russia. The hon. member for Three Rivers-St. Maurice (Mr. Bourgeois) has quoted the opinion of the president of the Catholic Union of Farmers in the province of Quebec in favour of this bill, and of course he approves of it entirely because ft is a government bill. But has he reflected that this bill is not only the most socialistic measure that to my knowledge has ever been presented in this parliament, but the one most imbued with the spirit of sovietism, especially that part which I have denounced? The creation of these local boards seems to have been borrowed from the legislation introduced in Russia for the creation of the sovietic local boards which control all local activities. They pretend that they leave each individual farmer to do what he pleases, but they make life impossible to him; the kulak has become a serf on his own land just as much as the member of the kolkhoz. Well, this bill is creating a
(Mr. Bourassa.]
replica of the kolkhoz under the komintern. Curiously enough that approval of the president of the Catholic Union of Farmers- the Catholic Union, mind you-appeared in the same paper which, the week previous, by the pen of an undoubtedly very honest and clever cleric, denounced the bolshevistic tendencies of Mr. Woodsworth and his party. I wonder if those same defenders of the faith and of social order, always on the alert to see cropping up the spirit of Lenin in the province of Quebec, will uphold the position taken by the hon. member for Three Rivers-St. Maurice and by the president of the Catholic Union of Farmers. If they do, if they remain silent in face of this legislation, then they will strengthen the opinion growing in the province of Quebec that these defenders of state, church and society, are much more concerned about the defence of the Tory party than of ordered society. It will be a new example of that display of zeal for religion which took place at the time an order in council was passed prohibiting the importation of Russian coal in order to enable Senator Webster and his associates to maintain their infernal monopoly in the city of Montreal, thereby reducing thousands of people to misery this last winter. And all that was done in the name of religion! But of course, when a large concern in the eastern part of the province wanted to import Russian oil, they were given a free hand. Religion was endangered by Russian coal coming to Montreal, but religion was in no danger from the importation of Russian oil to enable one of these mergers, so strongly and so properly denounced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, to make a little more money at the expense of the good people of the province of Quebec. It may look a little out of place, but in face of the kind of propaganda which has been carried on in Quebec for some weeks past, I have thought it my duty to protest and to show-I will not say the hypocrisy; no, I do not like such words- but to show the levity of mind of some people and the danger of fixed ideas. Some people have an obsession concerning Jews and bolshevists; everything good that happens has been in spite of the Jews and the bolshevists, and everything bad is their fault. I have no admiration for the bolshevists; I love the good Jews, such as my hon. friend here. I do not like the bad Jews any more than I do the bad Christians; but I do say that if we educate the good people of Quebec in such disregard of facts, facts economic, facts political and facts social, they will before long cease to be the vanguard of social order to whom the Prime Minister

Marketing Act-Mr. MacMillan (Saskatoon)
rendered such well deserved testimony in an interview he gave a few days ago. Once more I say:	Do not exploit religion and
prejudice when you are dealing with economic questions. Treat them on their merits, and pass the kind of legislation you should pass, without beclouding the issue.

speechtext:
First, Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the government and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) on the introduction of this bill. Having been interested practically all my life in the distribution of merchandise of all kinds, including the products of the farm, I sometimes wonder that the primary producer has got along as well as he has up to this time. If we look about us and then cast our minds back a few short years and see what has happened to the distributing system of this country I am sure we can come to no other conclusion than that the old distributing system has fallen down. The remarks I intend to make I think can be applied to the manner in which the primary producer has suffered in this country during the past number of years.
Let us consider for example what has happened to the wholesale drygoods trade, once a very great business. In Toronto when I was a young man, W. R. Brock & Company was a very big concern, and there were several others, John Macdonald & Company; Caldecott, Burton & Spence, Nisbett and Auld; Robert Darling; Greenshields of Montreal; Gault Brothers of Winnipeg and Montreal ; Robinson Little & Company of London and Winnipeg; Stobart of Winnipeg, and R. J. Whitla & Company of Winnipeg. What has happened to all these firms? Every one of them was doing a distributing business of not 'less than a million dollars a year. But what has happened? They have all gone out of business. The same thing applies to the boot and shoe business and, to some extent, to the grocery business, and, Mr. Speaker, the same thing applies to the primary producer at this time. If the system under which he has been operating for many years past is permitted to continue, the primary producer will go out of business also. It is a marvellous thing, when we think of it, having regard to the distributing system that has been in operation in this country, that we have done as well as we have. The records of Bradstreet and Dun are strewn with the wrecks of these institutions throughout the country, involving hundred of millions of dollars, yet this system has been permitted to continue. I must say
that it is my firm conviction, as one who has been in the retail business in a moderately large way for a number of years, as an independent in western Canada, that to some extent the manufacturers have been the architects of their own misfortune. They built up great institutions in this country and gave them secret rebates and concessions that an independent man could not get. The result has been that they have practically no independent men left; that is what it has come to to-day with the advent of the chain stores and branch department stores. That situation has been brought about to some extent by the system which has been employed by the manufacturers of this country, and more particularly by the manufacturers of eastern Canada.
The same thing applies to the manner in which the primary producer has been forced to market his products, and I say it is a good thing that to-day we have a bill going through this house that will give the primary producer some control over the way in which his products will be marketed to the ultimate consumer. I was amazed to hear the remarks of the hon. member for North Timiskaming (Mr. Bradette) the other day. The hon. gentleman said he was a retailer, yet he was concerned about what was going to happen to the ultimate consumer and as to what price the consumer would pay for the products he purchased if this bill came into effect. So far as I know, Mr. Speaker, the consumer in this country has always paid the price, but the primary producer has never received it. There are so many middle men who come in after the product leaves the farm and before it reaches the retail merchant and finally the ultimate consumer; there are so many profits all down the line that the consumer always pays the price.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, in the last few years and particularly up to 1930, we had mergers, amalgamations, maladministration of finances, financial racketeers and bucket shop gentlemen going through the country organizing this and that and merging this and that. To-day in the country there are scarcely any independent business men left, and as a result the primary producer finds himself forced to market a large percentage of his goods through these large institutions. So I think it is about time some sort of machinery should be set up by which the primary producer may have some control over the manner in which his goods are marketed, and I congratulate the minister upon having introduced this measure at this time.

Mr. Speaker, practically ninety-five per cent of our farm products are consumed within the oonfmes of our own country. I contend, and I think my statement can be substantiated, that our own home market is the best market we have. For that reason I say we should protect that market and do everything we can to help the farmers get every cent possible out of the amount paid by the ultimate consumer. Let us consider for a moment the man who grows potatoes, we will say, in eastern Canada. Let me say that I have sold potatoes brought from New Brunswick to Saskatchewan for $3 a bushel, but the farmer in New Brunswick did not get a very large share of the $3 that was paid in the province of Saskatchewan; in fact he did not get what he should have received when there is a short crop of potatoes in this part of the country. On the other hand when there is a short crop in eastern Canada and we have potatoes in western Canada they are shipped by brokers, jobbers and others and the fruit and vegetable dealers and hucksters get the profit instead of the farmers. As I see it the creation of this board is an attempt to direct that traffic and that business where it will bring the greatest return to the grower, and that is all we can reasonably expect. I do not say the bill is perfect; there is no doubt that it will be changed as time goes on, but at least it is an attempt to do something and I think a very great step in the interests of the primary producer.
For many years I have been amazed at the fruit growing industry of western Canada. Men have come to me in past years at their wits' end because of the condition of that industry; many of these men retired from the prairie provinces and went to live in British Columbia because of the climate. They were under the thumb of one of the greatest combines in this country, the Nash Fruit Company, which was fined some $200,000 in 1926 for some of the things it did, but which is still going strong, though now it is merged with a concern known as Western Grocers.

Some years ago a gentleman by the name of Mr. W. P. Riley, then of Port Arthur but later of Winnipeg, bought out the old A. McDonald Company of Winnipeg. He floated a great issue of shares on the market, which were purchased by the public; then the shares dropped to the point where they could not be sold at all. The chain store then came into the picture, and this gentleman established a chain known as the Red and White stores. Now he has these grocery stores all through the country. I do not know what sort of deal he made with them, but it would be interesting to find out.
At any rate this gentleman merged the Western Grocers with this Nash-Symington fruit combine, and to-day they control thirty-five distributing houses in western Canada. I am told that the ordinary brokerage fee on a car of fruit is about $10. I am informed on very good authority-I should say rather competent authority-that this concern collects as much as $40 and $50 per car. They go further; they collect secret rebates from the manufacturers of eastern Canada, and I understand that last year they placed in a special reserve account an amount in the neighbourhood of $100,000. What chance has the primary producer or the fruit grower in the province of British Columbia when he is up against a combination of that kind? So again I say I congratulate the minister on bringing in this measure which will give the primary producers throughout the length and breadth of this country at least a chance to better marketing conditions in connection with the products they grow.
I have been interested in the committee on price spreads and mass buying which from time to time has been holding meetings. In the city of Saskatoon I happen to be a shareholder in a stockyard company. If there Is one thing Mr. Speaker, more than another which affects the distribution of products of the primary producer it is in many instances the set up of distributing organizations. The committee would be well advised to go thoroughly into that branch of their investigations.
For a moment I should like to speak about the stockyard in my own city. May I say that I was somewhat instrumental in organizing or having organized the stockyard I have mentioned. Mr. H. P. Kennedy of Toronto, who is now president of the Union Stockyards of Saskatoon and president of the Edmonton Stockyards of Edmonton, and his manager, came to our city, and I hold in my hand an extract from a proposal which they laid before a number of business men of my city when

Marketing Act-Mr. MacMillan (Saskatoon)
in 1926 or 1927 they suggested to us, and we to them, that a stockyard should be organized in the city of Saskatoon. The extract is as follows:
It may be desirable however to have a few prominent men in the neighbourhood of the city of Saskatoon interested and a limited amount of stock will be available for them on the same basis as the other subscribers.
Then, I have before me the prospectus of the Union Stockyards of Saskatoon, Limited, in which I find the names of the following directors: H. P. Kennedy, live stock dealer, Toronto, president; Charles Bauckham, trust company manager, Toronto, vice-president; John L. Juhlin, stock yards manager, Edmonton; W. H. Adamson, insurance adjuster, Toronto, and J. H. S. Kerr, manager, Toronto. Norman Sommerville and Company of 67 Yonge Street, Toronto, are given as the solicitors, and the Dominion bank as the bankers. The point I am getting at is this, that the concern I have mentioned was organized and has done very excellent business from its inception. To-day it is beginning to pay and to pay handsomely. I am not so deeply interested in that particular feature, because those of us who put our money into the deal did not do so having in view any great dividends we might derive from it or any handsome returns which might come to us. We were more concerned with establishing a live stock industry in and about the city in which I live, and setting up facilities which would make possible the marketing of live stock on a little more profitable basis than in the past.
Then, as time goes on and the stockyard company begins to make money, what do we find? We must remember that this was one of those Simon pure companies, like many joint stock companies emanating from eastern Canada. Of course we were all to get a fair and even break-and in that statement I include the primary producer. But what do we find? Well, the president of the stockyard, the gentleman whose name I have given, drew a salary of $1,200-of course that is not a large salary; it does not amount to very much. The capital invested was about $58,-
000.	But last year, unknown to the shareholders at Saskatoon, he increased his salary by $2,500, bringing his total salary up to $3,700 -and that gentleman does nothing. He lives in the city of Toronto. The work is all done in Saskatoon because the yard is there, the cattle are there and the records are* kept there. This man does nothing, or practically nothing, and receives $3,700 for his services. The shareholders receive little or nothing. The directors, Toronto men, I presume obtain a commensurate amount for their services.
We decided we would like to have some information about this company, but we could not get it from the sources from which one would expect to obtain it, namely from the president or secretary of the company. Meeting with this difficulty we deputized a lawyer in Toronto to go out to Mr. Kennedy's office, which, by the way, was at that time at the union stockyards in Toronto, I suppose the Saskatoon company is being charged. rent, stenographic services and other charges made in connection with the Toronto office. What I am getting at is this, that in the final analysis all these charges are checked up against institutions in an endeavour to prove that certain businesses are not profitable, and that therefore the farmer should pay the rates that he does pay.
Not being able to obtain directly from the gentleman in question the information we sought, we asked the lawyer friend to interview Mr. Kennedy for the purpose of asking him certain questions. This is the lawyer's reply:
For about ten days before I left, I was in constant communication with Mr. Kennedy's office but could never get in touch with the man himself. Finally I made an appointment with him a few days ago. I attended at his office at the appointed time but he came outside of the office and said he was too busy to see me. I quickly asked him a few questions, and the storm started.
He was most unreasonable in his attitude, and shouted at the pitch of his voice. He told me he had consulted Mr. Norman Sommerville, K.C. as soon as he received a letter from you, as to the exact legal position. He had an interview with Mr. Sommerville, I believe, as he apparently knew who I was and seemed to resent my request to see the books. He said he was willing to allow me, as a representative of a shareholder, to inspect any books or documents of the company where there was any legal right to make such inspection. I told him that I was particularly anxious to find out from the books of the company the amounts which the directors had voted to themselves, and that I also wished to ascertain if the shareholders had ratified any such payments. He became livid when I made this request, and' said that he would tell the shareholders from a public platform in Saskatoon about October of this year anything they were entitled to ask. He also stated that if he saw you personally in Saskatoon, he might be willing to give you more information personally than he was inclined to give me as your representative.
He remarked you had not attended the shareholders' meeting where you could have obtained all the information which you desired.
I told him you could not attend a meeting in Toronto on account of the distance, and that he ought to give you all reasonable informaton by letter which you could' have obtained if you had been able to attend. He entirely disagreed

with this view, having in mind, no doubt, the Biblical quotation which you gave him in one of your letters. I asked him if he refused to give the information in regard to the directors' salaries, but he would not answer the question, stating that whatever my legal rights were, I would certainly receive my legal rights but nothing further. I could see no use in speaking to this man, so I left the office.

This letter is signed by Mr. James Cowan of Toronto, a lawyer in that city.
In the statement of the company for the year ended December 31, 1932, an item of $6,186.18 appears. True, this is not a large item, but we have been anxious to ascertain just what it covered and of what it is made up. The fact is that we could never get that information. Several letters were written in regard to the matter. However, having written only a few days ago I received a reply from Mr. Kennedy. The strange point is that the reply should have come just at this time when the price spreads committee is investigating all these matters. I was interested in a remark made by that gentleman the other day in the committee. He was asked this question and made this answer:
Q. You made a suggestion?
A. Under present conditions. This is the time when something wants to be done for the farmers of Canada. This is the time, gentlemen, to make men in Canada, not make fortunes.
That is his statement. According to his own letter, the item of $6,000 odd in this statement is made up of the shares purchased in the Edmonton Stockyards, Limited. He said:
With reference to the investment of $6,186.18 which appears in the statement of 1932. this represents the exact cost to the Union Stockyards of Saskatoon, Limited', for certain shares purchased in the Edmonton Stockyards, Limited.
I understand that for some time the Edmonton Stockyards Limited have not been doing very well and yet this company has been loaded up with shares which are not at all profitable. That is the way they hide some of the profits of this institution. I have before me the auditor's statement for the year ended December 31, 1932, signed by the presi-
(Mr. MacMillan.]
dent Mr. H. P. Kennedy and one of the directors, Mr. J. H. C. Kerr. The profit and loss account shows an income of $49,375.75 and expenses of operation, management and depreciation, $30,156.09. In my judgment that last item should be looked into and broken up, because I do not know how they could spend $30,156.09 on that business. That leaves a net operating profit of $19,219.68 and after deducting miscellaneous charges of $1,700 it leaves a net income of $17,457. The provision for dominion and provincial taxes is $2,679.56, which leaves a net income of $14,777.52. The president does nothing, but for argument's sake we will add his salary of $3,700. Without breaking up this item of expenses of operation, management and depreciation, $30,156.09, there is left a total profit of $18,477.22 on a capitalization or money paid in of $58,225. Ths is about thirty three and a third per cent profit on a stockyard business. If that other item is broken up I have no doubt it will be found that the profits of this stockyard are indeed very handsome. All this has a great bearing upon the price the primary producer receives for live stock passing through the stockyards. This gentleman is very much concerned and he wants legislation enacted to pass all live stock through the stockyards. He claims that prices are depressed if live stock goes direct to the packer. He may be quite right in that; I am not competent to judge, but I do know that if all live stock goes through the stockyards that gentleman will certainly get what is coming to him. In my judgment, that is all he is concerned about.
When we are considering the evidence given by these men engaged in different distributing businesses, we should endeavour to find out just what amount of money they are making out of the business in which they are concerned. I congratulate the minister on bringing forward this measure. It will give somebody the authority to investigate matters of this kind. It is not going to be left to the tender mercies of the farmer alone, as it is pretty difficult for him to do that sort of business by himself.
I have endeavoured to give the house an illustration of some of the things which go on in connection with the marketing of farm products under the present system. I hold in my hand a list of prices obtained for meats in tny own city. We have a relief store in that city and while I am not saying that that store is in the best interests of those on relief, the fact is that it is there.

Marketing Act-Miss Macphail
According to this return, in March, 1934, the relief store sold sirloin beef for ten cents per pound while the departmental stores charged twenty cents; for T-bone steaks the relief store charged ten cents per pound while the departmental stores charged twenty-one cents; for prime ribs the relief store charged ten cents while the departmental stores charged sixteen cents and the prices for shoulders were nine and twelve cents respectively. Such a spread is too great and it shows that the primary producer is not getting all of that to which he is entitled.
Without discussing the bill in detail, which will be done in committee, as I see it this bill is a move in the right direction. I think every hon. member should lend it his support in an endeavour to see that the primary producer gets more than what he has received in the past.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey):	Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to
say anything on this bill, as I expected we would vote to-night; but as it looks as though we shall not, I want to take just a moment or two to say that I intend to vote for the second reading of the bill.
There are several reasons why I intend to vote for the second reading. I do not think that the bill is a cure-all, but I do think it is the first step toward national planning. National planning is coming, although just how it will come may not be known to anyone. There must be some regulation in a world in which nation trades with nation rather than the individuals within a nation trading with each other. There must be some regulation in a world in which quotas exist. How can quotas be maintained unless there is some degree of control?
I have not been unduly disturbed by the black picture painted by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) in regard to the loss of personal and constitutional liberty. Economic liberty is more important, and unless we have it, all other liberties fall into insignificance. I have been surprised at the attitude taken by the official opposition, as I feel it is a mistaken attitude. I think the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) has expressed the attitude which should be adopted by all who represent agricultural constituencies. We should be willing to vote for the second reading of the bill, in the hope that those things which we do not like will be ironed out in committee of the whole.
I want to recommend to the official opposition an article by Sir Arthur Salter in the Atlantic Monthly of January of this year.
I believe he is a Liberal. In the summary of this article Sir Arthur says:
It is certain that, out of the stresses and strains of the present period, a system will ultimately emerge which will be substantially different from that to which we have been accustomed in the past. Economic activity will be planned and regulated, perhaps internationally, certainly nationally. The role of the state will be increasingly greater. It will have to transform its methods and equip itself for its new task. Its policy must be planned and not improvised.
That, in a couple of sentences, is how I feel about it. I think that economic activity will have to be planned and regulated, and this bill is an attempt to plan the marketing of natural products. It can be said, and I think fairly, that this bill may be used as an oppressive measure. That is true; it may be. We are taking a chance on the 'bill, because we cannot help doing so; but it is also true that the bill may provide the framework within which voluntary organizations may regulate the marketing of their own products. Whether some mistakes are made in the meantime or not remains to be seen, but I think that that will finally be done.
There are two other reasons why I shall support the second reading of the bill. In going over it I gather that the government is sympathetic to the cooperative enterprises of producers. I have been for a long time very much interested in cooperative enterprises as conducted by primary producers, and I think too that it may be, by following out the provisions of the bill, that the cooperative processing of natural products will be carried out with some government leadership and assistance. I have come to the conclusion, from having had something to do with cooperative processing, that until leadership is given by government, until there is real encouragement and assistance of one sort or another, it is impossible to carry on successfully cooperative processing establishments.
For all these reasons I am glad to support the second reading of the bill. It is not very often that I have the opportunity of supporting a measure brought down by the government, and therefore when the opportunity offers I seize it gladly. I have received, as I am sure all members have, a resolution from the Ontario Swine Breeders' Association asking for support to the bill. It is signed by people from six different counties in Ontario. And the Canadian Cooperative Live Stock Association have been for many months asking for a bill, if not like this one, at least something like it. I am of

Before the house adjourns there is a matter which I feel it my duty to call to its attention. In my unavoidable absence from the house for a short time this afternoon, the member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), in addressing the house on the second reading of Bill 51, made certain statements which I find unparliamentary. In that connection I would quote from May on Parliamentary Practice, 13th edition, page 316:
For preserving decency and order in debate, various rules have been laid down, which, in the Lords, are enforced by the house itself, and in the Commons by the Speaker in the first instance, and, if necessary, by the house. Any member may notice the violation of these rules, either by a cry of "order," or by rising in his place, and, in the Lords, addressing the house, and, in the Commons, the Speaker. When a member speaks to order, he must simply direct attention to the point complained of and submit it to the decision of the Speaker (see p. 338).
The rules for the conduct of debate divide themselves into two parts, viz.: such as are to be observed by members addressing the house; and those which have regard to the behaviour of members listening to the debate.
I would respectfully direct to the attention of hon. members these latter words of this authority on parliamentary (procedure:
-and those which have regard to the behaviour of members listening to the debate.
I have examined the official report of the debates and I find that the hon. member for Temiscouata, referring to the hon. member for Compton's support of the said bill, used these words: "To enable his brother to sell more jam he is ready to swallow any bill presented by this government," referring to the fact that the hon. member's brother sells jam to the Canadian National Railways, thus imputing motives different from those acknowledged. This is a reflection on the independence of a member of parliament. In this regard I would cite the same parliamentary authority, May, at page 325:
The use of temperate and decorous language is never more desirable than when a member is canvassing the opinions and conduct of his opponents in debate. The imputation of bad

motives, or motives different from those acknowledged; misrepresenting the language of another, or accusing him, in his turn, of misrepresentation; charging him with falsehood or deceit; or contemptuous or insulting language of any kind';-all these are unparliamentary, and call for prompt interference.
Speaking of the High Commissioner for Canada in England, the member for Temiscouata says: "Mr. Ferguson is acting in bad faith with the English people." As to that, I would quote from Bourinot, page 358:
All references to judges and courts of justice and to personages of high official station, of the nature of personal attacks and censure have always been considered unparliamentary and the speakers of the British and Canadian houses have always treated them as breaches of order. They have always insisted that, "Such expressions should be withdrawn."
The High Commissioner for Canada is in a high official position. He is appointed by authority of a special act of parliament, chapter 92, revised statutes of Canada. There are many precedents of such statements being held to be unparliamentary.
The hon. member for Temiscouata, applied to a member of the house, a word which is certainly not parliamentary. The dictionary gives the meaning of the word to be "a low term of abuse" and worse. The definition of this expression is so disgusting that I will not repeat it.
With the approval of the house I will instruct the editor of debates not to include the unparliamentary expressions used in the official report of to-day's debates.
